2

Compartment 2 — Irons, Forcible Entry & Air Bags

Driver's Side · Ground-level access · Forcible entry tools + extrication
Halligan Bar (Haligan)
What It Is
A heavy-duty steel bar approximately 30" long with three working ends: a fork (adz-like flat hook) on one end, a pick at a 90-degree angle to the fork, and a curved claw-fork on the opposite end. Designed by FDNY Chief Hugh Halligan in the 1940s, it is arguably the most important forcible entry tool ever made. It is almost always used as a matched pair with the flat-head axe — together this pair is called "the irons."
How to Use It
  1. Gap the door: Strike the fork end (adz end) into the door frame between the door and the jamb with the flat-head axe.
  2. Set the fork: Rotate the bar so the fork tines straddle the door frame around the locking bolt/latch area.
  3. Force the door: Apply rotational leverage by pushing the bar toward the door — the fork pries the door away from the jamb and defeats the lock.
  4. Pick end: Used to punch through doors, pry padlocks, or gain purchase in small openings.
  5. Claw end: Used for pulling ceilings, prying stubborn materials, and ventilation.
Why It's Needed
Rapid entry to locked or obstructed structures saves lives. Time spent fighting a door is time the fire is growing. The Halligan is designed to defeat outswing and inswing doors with threaded or mortise locks in seconds with the correct technique.
Also Known As
Halligan bar, haligan, hooligan tool, the bar, pro-bar, the irons (when paired with axe), the set.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
Before forcing entry: radio the IC, confirm you have the right address, and do a quick size-up of the door (outswing or inswing?). Forcing entry on the wrong side of a door or into a wind-driven fire scenario can create a blowtorch condition that kills the entry team. Know your door before you force it.
▶ WATCH IT IN ACTION
YouTube: "Halligan irons forcible entry training"
Flat Head Axe
What It Is
A firefighting axe with a flat striking face on one side and a sharpened axe blade on the other. The flat face is used as a striking tool (driving the Halligan). The blade is used for cutting, prying, and creating ventilation openings. This is the companion to the Halligan — "the irons" means this axe + the Halligan bar, working together.
How to Use It
  1. When working irons, the axe-person drives the Halligan fork into the door gap using the flat-head striking face.
  2. Once set, the axe person either assists with prying force or provides lighting and protection for the Halligan operator.
  3. As a cutting tool, use controlled, aimed swings for ventilation holes, wood cutting, or door panel removal.
  4. Always keep the blade covered when not in use — axe bags or sheaths prevent injury during transport.
Why It's Needed
The Halligan cannot drive itself into a door gap. The flat-head axe is the force multiplier that makes the Halligan work. Together, one team of two firefighters with irons can force most residential doors in under 30 seconds.
Also Known As
Flat-head axe, flat head, fire axe, FHA, the axe (when carried with Halligan), part of "the irons."
Maul
What It Is
A heavy two-headed striking tool with a wedge shape on one end and a flat sledgehammer-style face on the other end. This is different from a sledgehammer — a sledgehammer has flat striking faces on both ends; the maul has a wedge on one end specifically for splitting and prying-driving applications. In the fire service, the maul is used as an alternative to the flat-head axe for driving the Halligan when extreme force is required, or for breaching walls, breaking through security doors and commercial steel doors, splitting wood members, and other high-force impact work.
How to Use It
Hold the handle with two hands, use controlled swings to drive the Halligan or strike materials. Do not swing overhead in low-ceiling spaces — you'll hit the ceiling and lose control of the tool. Stay square to the target for accuracy.
Why It's Needed
Commercial structures, security doors, and padlocked gates require more force than a flat-head axe can deliver. The maul also pairs with the Halligan on heavy-duty forcible entry scenarios where a standard axe strike isn't getting the bar set.
Also Known As
Maul, force maul, splitting maul, wedge-and-flat striking tool. Note: a maul is NOT a sledgehammer — sledgehammers have two flat faces; mauls have a wedge + a flat.
Closet Pike Pole (D Handle)
What It Is
A short-handled pike pole (typically 4–6 feet) with a "D" handle on the butt end, designed to be used in confined spaces like closets, attic access areas, and smaller rooms where a full-length pike pole would be unmanageable. The D handle gives a two-handed grip for added leverage in tight spots. It has the same metal head as a regular pike pole: a sharp point and a sharpened hook.
How to Use It
Use the point to punch into ceilings, walls, and floors to check for hidden fire extension. Use the hook to pull down ceiling materials, lath and plaster, or drywall to expose concealed spaces. In overhaul, systematically open concealed spaces — fire travels in walls, floors, and attic spaces.
Why It's Needed
Fire hides. A fully knocked-down fire that has extended into a wall or ceiling cavity will re-ignite hours later if not fully opened up and extinguished. The closet pike pole is your tool for checking small, confined areas without needing full extension.
Also Known As
Short pike pole, closet hook, drywall hook, overhaul hook, short hook, D-handle pike, D-handle hook.
Bolt Cutters — Medium & Large ×1 each
What They Are
Heavy-duty cutting tools with compound-action pivot systems and hardened steel cutting jaws. The medium cutter has a hook feature for catching and cutting barbed wire. The large cutter is for heavy-gauge padlocks, chain-link fence, and heavy chains. Stored on the inside of the swinging door of Comp 2.
How to Use Them
  1. Position the jaws around the material to be cut — engage as close to the pivot as possible for maximum leverage (the closer to the pivot, the more force the jaws apply).
  2. Apply firm, steady squeezing pressure — avoid jerking or twisting which can damage the jaws.
  3. If the padlock is hardened steel, do NOT try to cut the lock with bolt cutters — bolt cutters cannot cut hardened steel. Instead, cut the chain link or hasp the lock is securing. The chain link is almost always softer steel than the padlock body.
  4. For non-hardened padlock shackles, cut both sides of the shackle rather than the body.
  5. For barbed wire, use the hook on the medium cutter to capture the wire before cutting.
Why They're Needed
Access control. Locked gates, chained fences, padlocked doors, and security cables are common barriers between you and victims. Bolt cutters are the fastest non-powered solution for most lock and chain scenarios.
Also Known As
Bolt cutters, bolt croppers, chain cutters, lock cutters.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — HARDENED STEEL
Bolt cutters cannot cut hardened steel padlock shackles. If you suspect a hardened-steel padlock, attack the chain link or the hasp instead — both are usually softer than the lock itself. Trying to force-cut hardened steel will spring or wreck your bolt cutters.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
Do not attempt to cut electrical cable, energized wire, or anything you can't positively identify as non-electrical. Always assume any cable near a structure fire or rescue may be energized until confirmed otherwise by the utility or a meter reading.
K-Tool in Leather Case
What It Is
The K-Tool is a specialized lock-pulling device shaped like the letter K. It's inserted over a commercial door lock cylinder, locked in place, and then driven by the Halligan bar to extract (pull) the entire lock cylinder from the door — exposing the locking mechanism and allowing the door to be opened without major damage to the door itself.
How to Use It
  1. Slide the K-Tool over the lock cylinder — it grips the cylinder on two sides.
  2. Hook the Halligan bar's fork end through the K-Tool's drive ring.
  3. Apply outward (pulling) force with the Halligan while a second firefighter strikes the Halligan from behind with the flat-head axe.
  4. The cylinder pulls out, exposing the tumbler mechanism.
  5. Use a screwdriver or the pick of the Halligan to actuate the exposed mechanism and open the lock.
Why It's Needed
Commercial structures with high-security lock cylinders (mortise locks, deadbolts, Medeco-type locks) resist conventional door forcing. The K-Tool defeats these by removing the cylinder rather than forcing the bolt — faster and with less collateral damage on non-fire entries.
Also Known As
K-tool, key tool, cylinder puller, lock puller.
▶ WATCH IT IN ACTION
YouTube: "K-Tool lock cylinder pull forcible entry"
Manhole Cover Remover
What It Is
A specialized hook or lifting tool designed to engage the recessed holes or edges of a cast iron manhole cover and lift it safely. These covers weigh 100–250 lbs and are designed to be flush with the road surface, making them nearly impossible to lift with bare hands or regular tools.
How to Use It
Insert the hook end into the lift hole on the manhole cover, stand clear of the opening direction, and lift using legs, not back. Slide the cover to the side rather than lifting completely clear — it's heavy and a drop back into the hole is a hazard to anyone working below.
Why It's Needed
Underground utility fires, confined space rescues, victim entrapment in drainage systems, and access to underground vaults all require opening manhole covers. The specialized tool makes this safe and fast.
Also Known As
Manhole hook, manhole lifter, lid hook, cover puller.
Air Bags — Lifting Bags ×1–2 in Comp 2
What They Are
High-pressure pneumatic lifting bags made of reinforced neoprene or similar material. When inflated, they generate enormous lifting force — some bags can lift 20–75 tons depending on size. They are inflated from SCBA air tanks or a dedicated air supply and controlled by the orange controller box (stored in Comp 3). On E62, both bags may occasionally be in Comp 2 rather than Comp 3. Max inflation pressure: 118 PSI — do not exceed.
How to Use Them
  1. Size up the load and determine bag placement — bags should be inserted into openings at least as wide as the deflated bag thickness.
  2. Insert bags into the void space under the load.
  3. Connect the air supply hose to the bag and to the orange controller.
  4. Inflate slowly in small increments — never inflate beyond 118 PSI.
  5. Crib as you go — place cribbing (wooden blocks, see Comp 3) under the load as it rises.
  6. Never work under a load supported only by air bags — always have cribbing in place.
Why They're Needed
Vehicle extrication, structural collapse rescue, and lifting heavy objects off trapped victims. A car can weigh 3,000–5,000 lbs. A collapsed floor section can pin a victim under hundreds of pounds. Air bags provide controlled, safe, powerful lifting without power equipment.
Also Known As
Air bags, lifting bags, high-pressure bags, pneumatic bags, rescue bags.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — NEVER EXCEED 118 PSI
Overinflating an air bag can cause catastrophic bag failure, ejecting the load and injuring rescuers. The 118 PSI limit is a hard safety ceiling — both E61 and E62 use this same limit. Also: never stack more than two bags directly on top of each other — unstacked bags are unstable and can eject sideways under load.
▶ WATCH IT IN ACTION
YouTube: "high-pressure air bag rescue lifting cribbing"
Air Tanks ×3 — Outside of Comp 2
What They Are
Spare SCBA (Self-Contained Breathing Apparatus) air cylinders stored on the outside of Compartment 2. These are the replaceable part of your breathing air system — when your on-mask cylinder runs low, you swap to a fresh one.
How to Use Them
  1. Check pressure gauge on each bottle during compartment check — should be at full working pressure (typically 4,500 PSI for carbon fiber cylinders).
  2. To swap a cylinder, exit the IDLH, deactivate the SCBA, remove the spent bottle (quarter-turn counterclockwise to remove), install fresh bottle (quarter-turn clockwise to seat and seal).
  3. Activate and test before re-entry.
Why They're Needed
Air supply is the single most critical limiting factor for interior firefighting. A standard 45-minute SCBA cylinder in actual working conditions often lasts 20–25 minutes. Spare tanks allow crews to continue operations at prolonged incidents without waiting for cylinder deliveries from the station.
Also Known As
Air bottle, SCBA cylinder, tank, bottle, spare air, spare cylinder.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
During compartment check, every air bottle must be checked for pressure AND that the valve is fully open. A full bottle with a closed valve is the same as an empty bottle — you won't know until you're inside and it's too late.
↑ Back to top
3

Compartment 3 — RIT, Rescue & Ventilation

Driver's Side · RIT Pack, Air Bags, Fan, Cellar Nozzle
TOP SHELF
RIT Pack — Rapid Intervention Team Pack 60-min, 4500 PSI
What It Is
A pre-assembled rescue pack carried by the Rapid Intervention Team — a dedicated crew staged outside the structure whose sole job is to rescue a downed or trapped firefighter. This pack contains: a six-foot hose section (to extend air supply to a downed firefighter), an extra SCBA unit, Universal Air Connection (UCA) fitting, buddy breathing connectors, a 60-minute duration cylinder at 4,500 PSI. This is on E62 but not on E61.
How to Use It
  1. RIT deploys when a firefighter MAYDAY is declared — do not activate until ordered or MAYDAY is confirmed.
  2. Team enters with the pack and locates the downed firefighter.
  3. Connect the UCA fitting to the downed firefighter's SCBA low-pressure port — this bypasses their regulator and supplies emergency air directly.
  4. Buddy connector allows a firefighter to share air with a distressed crewmate while moving them to safety.
  5. The 6-foot hose section gives reach to connect air without having to reposition the entire pack.
Why It's Needed
Every working structure fire requires a RIT. Every single one, regardless of size. NFPA 1710 and OSHA 2-in/2-out requirements exist because firefighters die in structures. When a MAYDAY comes, the RIT is the last line between life and death for that firefighter. You need to know this pack cold — ideally in the dark, in a mask, under stress.
Also Known As
RIT pack, RIC pack (Rapid Intervention Crew), FAST pack (Firefighter Assist and Search Team), rescue air pack, emergency air supply, EBSS (Emergency Breathing Support System).
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
The RIT pack is not a staging item — it must be carried by a designated team to the entry point of the structure and staged immediately upon arrival. A RIT pack sitting in the compartment when a MAYDAY is declared is useless. On E62, this is your responsibility to know and verify.
▶ WATCH IT IN ACTION
YouTube: "RIT pack MAYDAY rapid intervention team training"
MIDDLE SHELF
Portable Work Lights ×2
What They Are
Battery-powered or electric portable floodlights that illuminate large areas at night or in low-visibility conditions. Typically LED panels or flood units on adjustable stands or hooks. The note on E62 is to make sure they're plugged in — these are likely corded units that charge via the apparatus electrical system.
Why They're Needed
Nighttime operations, post-fire overhaul, vehicle accidents in unlit areas, and any scene where scene lighting is inadequate. Working in the dark is dangerous — good lighting improves situational awareness, reduces errors, and protects crews from trip and fall hazards.
Also Known As
Work lights, scene lights, portable lights, flood lights, drop lights.
💡 COMPARTMENT CHECK NOTE
The document specifically says "make sure it's plugged in" for the ventilation fan — but this applies to your work lights too. During your daily compartment check, confirm corded/rechargeable equipment is actually plugged into the apparatus charging circuit. A dead work light at 0200 is worse than useless.
Cellar Nozzle on Cellar Pipe
What It Is
A specialized nozzle assembly designed for fighting basement and cellar fires from the floor above. The cellar pipe is a curved metal tube that gets inserted through a small hole cut in the floor. The cellar nozzle at its end spins (driven by water pressure) and sprays water in a 360-degree pattern, flooding the space below without requiring anyone to descend into the fire area.
How to Use It
  1. Cut or locate a small access hole in the floor above the basement fire.
  2. Lower the cellar pipe and nozzle through the hole.
  3. Connect your attack line to the inlet of the cellar pipe.
  4. Flow water — the spinning nozzle disperses water throughout the cellar space.
  5. Do not advance into the cellar until the fire is knocked down and conditions are evaluated.
Why It's Needed
Basement fires are among the most dangerous scenarios in residential firefighting. Fire burning below the floor you're standing on is burning through your means of support. A cellar nozzle lets you apply water to a below-grade fire without sending firefighters into a potentially floor-collapse scenario.
Also Known As
Cellar nozzle, cellar pipe, rotary nozzle, whirling nozzle, basement nozzle.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
Basement fires demand extreme caution about floor integrity. If the fire has been burning long enough to char the joists supporting your floor, that floor can fail suddenly. Sound the floor before advancing — use your tool, your foot, and your eyes. The cellar nozzle exists precisely to let you fight this fire without betting your life on a compromised floor.
▶ WATCH IT IN ACTION
YouTube: "cellar nozzle basement fire attack"
BOTTOM SHELF
Ventilation Fan (Battery Powered, Positive Pressure Ventilation)
What It Is
A battery-powered high-output blower fan used to force fresh air into a structure and push smoke, heat, and toxic gases out. This is called Positive Pressure Ventilation (PPV) or Positive Pressure Attack (PPA). Because it runs on a battery, you can deploy it instantly — no extension cord to run, no generator to start. The fan is placed outside a doorway and angled to cover the entire door opening, creating positive air pressure inside the structure that pushes contaminated atmosphere out through an exhaust opening on the opposite side.
How to Use It
  1. Identify your inlet (entry door) and exhaust opening (window, vent, opening on opposite side).
  2. Place the fan approximately 8–10 feet from the door opening, angled to cover the full doorframe — the air cone should slightly exceed the door perimeter.
  3. Open the exhaust opening on the far side of the structure before starting the fan.
  4. Start the fan and confirm positive pressure — smoke should move toward the exhaust.
  5. Coordinate fan operation with your IC and attack team.
Why It's Needed
Smoke is toxic, hot, and obscures visibility. PPV removes it faster and more completely than traditional hydraulic or natural ventilation. It improves conditions for crews, improves victim survivability, and dramatically reduces property damage by clearing smoke from uninvolved areas.
Also Known As
PPV fan, positive pressure fan, smoke fan, electric fan, ventilation fan, blower, the fan.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
Never use PPV on an uncontrolled fire without IC approval. Adding fresh oxygen to a compartment fire can intensify the fire rapidly. PPV is a coordinated tactic — used improperly it can push fire toward victims or crews. Also: confirm the fan is plugged into the apparatus charging circuit during non-use so it starts when you need it.
Orange Box — Air Bag Controller
What It Is
The control manifold for the pneumatic air bags. It's a regulator-and-valve assembly (typically orange-colored for visibility) that connects your air supply (SCBA tank) to one or two air bags, allowing controlled, regulated inflation. It includes pressure gauges, individual bag valves, and a safety relief valve.
How to Use It
  1. Connect the SCBA cylinder to the controller's inlet fitting.
  2. Connect the air bags to the outlet ports — each bag has its own hose and port.
  3. Open the SCBA cylinder valve — watch the supply gauge rise.
  4. Open bag valves slowly and in small increments — inflate bags a few inches at a time while cribbing underneath.
  5. Monitor bag pressure gauges — never exceed 118 PSI.
  6. To deflate: close the bag valve and open the relief/exhaust.
Why It's Needed
You cannot safely inflate air bags without a regulator. Direct SCBA tank pressure (4,500 PSI) connected directly to an air bag would rupture it instantly. The controller steps pressure down and gives you precise control over inflation rate and pressure.
Also Known As
Air bag controller, control box, manifold, regulator, orange box.
Cribbing (Plastic)
What It Is
Short blocks of plastic (engineered polymer) cribbing — used to build stable, stacking supports under lifted or displaced loads during rescue operations. Plastic cribbing is more reliable than wood cribbing: it can be tested to a known specific load rating, it doesn't rot, it doesn't absorb fluids, and the strength is standardized across every block (so the engineering values you trust on Block #1 are exactly the same on Block #50). Wood cribbing varies block-to-block — it can rot internally, get waterlogged, or split along a hidden grain. Cribbing goes hand-in-hand with air bags and hydraulic tools — as you lift, you crib. The load is always supported by cribbing, never by equipment alone.
How to Use It
Build a "box crib" by alternating layers of wood at 90-degree angles, like a log cabin — this creates maximum stability and bearing surface. As a load is lifted an inch, slide cribbing underneath. Never allow the load to be fully supported only by air bags or jacks — always have cribbing at every lift increment.
Why It's Needed
Air bags can fail. Hydraulic jacks can leak down. A vehicle can shift. If any of these happen with a victim under a load and no cribbing in place, the result is fatal. Cribbing is the passive, fail-safe support that protects the victim and the rescuers regardless of equipment failure.
Also Known As
Plastic cribbing, crib blocks, shoring blocks, polymer crib, step chocks (step-shaped pre-cut wedge version).
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — "CRIB AS YOU GO"
This phrase should be burned into your brain. Every half-inch of lift gets a half-inch of crib placed under the load before the next lift. There is no acceptable exception to this. A rescuer who skips cribbing to "get it done faster" is gambling with a victim's life.
Transformer Nozzles
What They Are
Specialized nozzles designed to spray water into small openings or enclosed spaces — think: injection firefighting. They typically attach to a standard hose coupling and allow water to be directed into a wall cavity, ceiling void, locked room, or any space too small or too dangerous to enter. Also called "penetrating nozzles" or "piercing nozzles" in some configurations.
How to Use Them
Insert the nozzle tip into the target opening (or drill/punch a hole first). Connect the attack line and flow water into the concealed space. The nozzle distributes water throughout the void to knock down hidden fire. Particularly effective in wall fires, concealed ceiling fires, and attic fires where structural penetration is not needed.
Why They're Needed
Opening walls with tools is time-consuming and creates structural damage. Where possible, injecting water through a small hole is faster and less destructive while still knocking down hidden fire extension.
Also Known As
Transformer nozzle, piercing nozzle, penetrating nozzle, injection nozzle, Elkhart nozzle, Hi-Combat nozzle.
↑ Back to top
R

Rear of Truck — Left Panel, Center & Rescue Tools

Hurst Tools, Hydraulic Ram, Reciprocating Saw, Ladders, NY Hooks
LEFT OF REAR — HOOKS & LADDER
New York Hooks ×2 — 6 ft & 8 ft
What They Are
Also called "New York" or "Drywall" hooks. Long-handled tools with a large, angled hook-and-rake head that are used aggressively to pull down ceilings, drywall, lath and plaster, and other construction materials during overhaul and ventilation. Unlike a pike pole with a point-and-hook tip, the NY hook has a wide, raking head designed to pull large sections at once.
How to Use Them
  1. Select appropriate length for the space (6 ft for lower ceilings, 8 ft for higher).
  2. Insert the hook head above ceiling material and pull down with controlled, deliberate force.
  3. Work systematically — open ceiling systematically to reveal the full extent of fire spread.
  4. Stay out of the fall zone of material being pulled down — ceiling debris can be hot, heavy, and sharp.
Why They're Needed
Overhaul is the most underrated part of fire operations. Hidden fire in walls and ceilings causes fatalities long after the main fire appears controlled. NY hooks are designed to open construction material quickly so you can see and extinguish hidden fire.
Also Known As
New York hook, drywall hook, NY hook, overhaul hook, plaster hook, San Francisco hook (different head variant), combination hook.
Attic Ladder 10 ft
What It Is
A short, lightweight folding or extension ladder — typically aluminum — designed to fit through a standard attic access hatch (22"×30") and extend enough to allow a firefighter to climb safely into the attic space. At 10 feet, it provides access to attics with floor-level hatches up to approximately 8–9 feet off the ground.
How to Use It
Open the attic hatch, extend the ladder to appropriate length (if adjustable), set the base securely on the floor, and lean the upper end against or through the opening. A spotter should secure the base while the firefighter ascends. Do not climb into an attic space without your SCBA in place if any possibility of fire or smoke exists.
Why It's Needed
Attic fires are a common and serious extension risk. You can't fight or check an attic fire you can't access. The attic ladder provides safe access through standard pull-down hatches without needing to cut the ceiling or use a full extension ladder.
Also Known As
Attic ladder, folding ladder, access ladder, multi-position folding ladder.
MIDDLE OF REAR — RESCUE TOOLS
Hurst Rescue Cutter & Hurst Rescue Spreader
What They Are
Hurst Spreader ("The Jaws"): Hydraulically-powered tool with two blades that spread apart or squeeze together with tremendous force. Used to pry open vehicle doors, displace steering wheels, and create access to trapped vehicle occupants.

Hurst Cutter ("The Cutters"): Hydraulically-powered cutting tool — essentially industrial scissors — used to cut vehicle A, B, and C pillars, door hinges, seat belts, and structural elements of vehicle bodies. Together, the spreader creates space and the cutter removes obstructions.
How to Use Them
  1. Connect to the hydraulic power unit (battery-powered or engine-powered).
  2. Stabilize the vehicle first — chock wheels, deflate tires if needed, use cribbing.
  3. Spreader: Insert tips into the door gap at the latch or hinge, spread to pop the door.
  4. Cutter: Position jaws fully around the target — partial cuts on structural steel cause dangerous blade deflection. Cut all at once.
  5. Always cover glass before cutting metal near occupants.
Why They're Needed
Modern vehicle construction — high-strength steel, airbags, complex geometry — makes manual extrication virtually impossible in serious crashes. Hurst tools are purpose-designed to cut and spread vehicle structures that no manual tool can defeat.
Also Known As
Jaws of Life (trade name, technically refers to the spreader), spreader, cutters, Hurst tools, hydraulic rescue tools, extrication tools, combination tool (when it's a single cutter/spreader unit).
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
Never cut the roof post nearest the victim's head without confirming EVERY airbag has deployed and the system is fully depowered. Cutting a structural pillar with an undeployed side curtain or seat-mounted airbag can cause it to detonate into the victim and rescuers. Always disconnect the battery when possible before cutting structural components.
▶ WATCH IT IN ACTION
YouTube: "Hurst jaws of life vehicle extrication training"
Hydraulic Ram
What It Is
A hydraulic cylinder that extends under power to push or spread materials apart. Where the spreader pries in a V-shape, the ram pushes in a linear direction — it can displace a steering column, push a firewall back, or force structural elements apart that are too restricted for the spreader tips to fit into.
How to Use It
Connect to the hydraulic power unit. Position the ram base against a solid structural anchor and the extension tip against the target. Extend slowly with controlled force. Use the Quick Kick ram support (silver bracket with teeth) to hold the ram stable when positioning in a vehicle or structure without a natural anchor point.
Why It's Needed
Not every rescue can be solved with spreading or cutting. Sometimes you need directed linear force — pushing a dashboard off a trapped leg, pushing a door frame away from a pinned door, or extending space along a single axis. The ram fills this gap.
Also Known As
Ram, hydraulic ram, push ram, power ram, porta-power (informal for general hydraulic tools).
Reciprocating Saw (Battery Powered)
What It Is
A battery-powered saw (no AC cord — battery only on this rig) with a blade that moves in a reciprocating (back-and-forth) motion. Unlike a circular saw (round blade spinning) or chainsaw, the reciprocating saw is highly maneuverable, operates in confined spaces, and can cut wood, metal, plastic, and composite materials depending on blade selection.
Changing Blades
  1. Make sure the saw is OFF and the battery is removed before changing blades — the trigger lock is not enough.
  2. Rotate the keyless blade clamp collar at the front of the saw to its open position (most modern saws release with a quarter-turn — no wrench needed).
  3. Pull the old blade straight out.
  4. Insert the new blade with teeth facing the direction you'll be cutting (typically teeth-down for most cuts).
  5. Release the collar — it should snap back and lock the blade in place. Tug the blade to confirm it's seated.
Replacing the Battery
  1. Slide the depleted battery off the saw's battery foot (release the latch — usually a single button or thumb tab).
  2. Take a freshly charged battery from the rig's battery rack.
  3. Slide it onto the foot until it clicks into place.
  4. Test-trigger the saw briefly to confirm power before bringing it to work.
  5. Return the depleted battery to the charger so the next crew has a charged spare.
How to Use It
  1. Select correct blade for the material — wood blades, metal blades, and combination blades are different.
  2. Insert the blade fully and confirm it's locked before operation.
  3. Start the saw before contacting the material — contact starting can bind or kick back.
  4. Use steady forward pressure — let the blade do the work, don't force it.
  5. Keep your free hand clear of the blade path at all times.
Why It's Needed
Rescue situations involving seatbelts, aircraft skin, vehicle floors, structural lumber, and security bars all require rapid cutting. The reciprocating saw handles most of these. It's also lighter and more maneuverable than a chainsaw in confined rescue environments.
Also Known As
Reciprocating saw, Sawzall (Milwaukee trade name — extremely common in fire service), recip saw, demo saw, sabre saw.
Window Punch
What It Is
A small spring-loaded punch device — the size of a large marker — with a hardened steel tip. When pressed against a vehicle's tempered glass window (side or rear windows, not laminated windshield) and the mechanism is activated, it releases a concentrated impact that causes the glass to shatter into thousands of small, relatively harmless pieces.
How to Use It
  1. Position the tip firmly in one of the lower corners of the tempered glass window.
  2. Push firmly to activate the spring mechanism — the tip strikes the glass with concentrated force.
  3. The glass will "dice" into small cubes — use a gloved hand or tool to clear the remaining glass.
  4. Clear the frame of glass shards before reaching inside near the victim.
Why It's Needed
Speed. Manual window breaking with a tool risks injuring the victim inside with flying glass or tool entry. A window punch breaks tempered glass cleanly and quickly in any confined space. Essential for vehicle rescue and locked vehicle/child entrapment calls.
Also Known As
Window punch, life hammer, glass punch, spring punch, center punch, ResQMe (popular trade name).
🔰 ROOKIE MISTAKE
Trying to use the window punch on a laminated windshield — it won't work. Windshields are laminated safety glass, which holds together when broken. Window punches only work on tempered glass (side and rear windows). Use the Halligan, axe, or saw on windshields.
Batteries ×6 Upper Shelf + Battery-to-AC Converter
What They Are
Six rechargeable batteries for the power tools (Hurst tools, reciprocating saw, possibly lights). The battery-to-AC converter (starred heavily in the document) is a critical item — it converts battery power to standard 120V AC current, allowing corded equipment to operate off the apparatus batteries in the field.
Why It's Needed
Modern battery-powered rescue tools are only as good as their charge. Having six batteries means you can sustain extended rescue operations without power loss. The AC converter extends capability to any 110V device in the field — charging medical equipment, running lights, powering small tools — without needing shore power or a generator.
Also Known As
Batteries, power packs, tool batteries; AC converter: inverter, battery inverter, mobile AC.
⚠ COMPARTMENT CHECK — BATTERY STATUS
All six batteries should be seated in their chargers during non-use. During your daily check, verify charge status on each battery. Fully charged, all six. A dead battery discovered mid-extrication is a critical failure. The document flags the AC converter with multiple asterisks — it is important, it is easily overlooked, check it.
Backboards ×2 — Rear Mounted
What They Are
Rigid plastic (or wooden — older style) long spine boards used for immobilizing patients with suspected spinal injuries during rescue and transport. Usually 6 feet long, they include handholds around the perimeter and strap attachment points.
How to Use Them
Log-roll or slide the patient onto the board while maintaining spinal alignment. Secure with straps across chest, abdomen, and legs. Apply a cervical collar first if possible. Multiple rescuers are typically needed for safe application.
Why They're Needed
Spinal cord injuries are irreversible. Any trauma patient with a mechanism of injury (fall, vehicle crash, violence) that could involve spinal forces needs to be immobilized until cleared by medical personnel. The backboard provides that immobilization during extraction and transport.
Also Known As
Backboard, long board, spine board, LSB (long spine board), trauma board.
↑ Back to top
5

Compartment 5 — Officer's Side

Axes, Search Rope, Water Rescue Throw, Tools
TOP SHELF — AXE COMPLEMENT
💡 KNOW YOUR AXES
Engine 62 carries four different axes. Don't just know they're there — know the difference and when each one is preferred. Comp 5 (officer side) carries a complete set; there is also a flat-head axe in Comp 2 (driver's side). Axe knowledge is a fundamental fireground competency.
Pick Head Axe / Fire Axe
What It Is
The classic fire service axe: a wood or fiberglass handle with a head featuring a sharp axe blade on one side and a hardened steel pick (spike) on the other. The "pick head" distinguishes it from the flat-head axe — the pick is used for penetrating, prying, and hooking materials. This is the axe most people picture when they think "firefighter."
How to Use It
Blade end for cutting wood, creating ventilation holes, and chopping. Pick end for punching through materials, hooking into ceilings for pulling, prying away materials, and creating a starting point for the Halligan bar. Also used to strike the Halligan in forcible entry (though the flat-head is preferred for this).
Why It's Needed
Dual-purpose cutting and penetrating capability in a single tool. The pick gives you a prying/punching capability that the flat-head lacks.
Also Known As
Pick head axe, pick axe (informally), fire axe, firefighter's axe, the pick head.
Pig Axe
What It Is
A combination striking tool — pick on one side, flat head on the other. The Pig Axe is typically referred to on the radio and around the firehouse as "the Pig" or "the Pig Tool." All three names point to the same hand tool. This is NOT the Pig Drain Cover — that's a completely different item (a flexible rubber mat used to seal storm drains during hazmat / runoff containment). Three names, one tool — but watch out for the drain cover with a similar name.
Why It's Needed
Versatility in a compact tool. The Pig Axe handles overhaul, ventilation, and light forcible entry without carrying multiple separate tools. Good for roof operations, closet overhaul, and confined-space work.
Also Known As
The Pig, Pig Tool, Pig Axe, combination striking tool. NOT the Pig Drain Cover (which is a separate item — see Comp 5).
💡 NAMING — DON'T GET CONFUSED
"The Pig" / "Pig Tool" / "Pig Axe" = the striking tool. "Pig Drain Cover" = a separate item, the rubber drain mat. They share part of a name and live on the same rig — don't conflate them when somebody hollers for "the pig."
MIDDLE SHELF
RASP — 200 ft Search Rope
What It Is
RASP (Rapid Anchor Search Package) or search rope — a 200-foot guideline rope for interior search operations in zero-visibility environments. The rope has beads at regular intervals and a butterfly knot at 100 feet, allowing firefighters to maintain orientation, track their distance of travel, and communicate their position to crew members outside.
How to Use It
  1. Anchor the bag end (the starting end) at a fixed point at the entry — a doorknob, stair railing, or structural anchor.
  2. The search team pays out rope as they advance into the structure.
  3. The bead markers at intervals tell you how far you've traveled from the anchor.
  4. The butterfly knot at 100 ft is a tactile signal in the dark — "you're halfway."
  5. To return, follow the rope back to the anchor — never let go of the rope in zero visibility.
Why It's Needed
Search operations in zero-visibility smoke conditions are disorienting even for experienced firefighters. The search rope gives you a physical lifeline to follow back out. Firefighters have died of disorientation in smoke-filled buildings — the search rope is a critical life-safety tool.
Also Known As
Search rope, RASP, guideline, tag line, Denver Drill rope (training context), personal search line.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
The rope is only useful if it's anchored before you advance. A common error is walking the rope in without securing the anchor end — now you have a coil of rope in the building and no way out. Anchor first, advance second. Every time.
▶ WATCH IT IN ACTION
YouTube: "search rope interior firefighting zero visibility"
Pig Drain Cover
What It Is
A large, flexible rubber cover designed to fit over storm drains, manholes, or floor drains to prevent contaminated water (from firefighting runoff, chemical spills, or hazmat incidents) from entering the drainage system. The Pig Drain Cover is NEVER referred to as "the Pig." "The Pig" / "Pig Tool" / "Pig Axe" all refer to the striking tool — a completely different item. When someone says "grab the pig," they want the axe. When they want this drain mat, they'll say "Pig Drain Cover" or "drain cover."
How to Use It
Place the flexible cover over the drain opening. The weight and flexibility of the rubber creates a seal. Push down on the edges to ensure full contact. For flowing water situations, use with sandbags or other weight to maintain the seal under pressure.
Why It's Needed
Environmental compliance. Firefighting runoff contains carcinogens, heavy metals from combustion, and chemical contaminants. Environmental regulations in most jurisdictions prohibit uncontrolled discharge of fireground runoff into storm drains. The Pig Drain Cover is your first line of environmental protection on scene.
Also Known As
Pig Drain Cover, drain cover, drain plug, storm drain cover, environmental plug. NEVER "the Pig" — that name is reserved for the Pig Axe.
BOTTOM SHELF
Red Bag — 4 PFDs + 1 Throw Preserver
What They Are
PFD (Personal Flotation Device): Life vests/jackets that keep a person afloat in water. Four are stored for crew use in water rescue scenarios.

Throw Preserver / Ring Buoy: A ring-shaped flotation device attached to a throw line. Thrown to a distressed swimmer or victim, they grab it and you pull them to safety — without entering the water yourself.
How to Use Them
PFD: Put it on before entering or near the water — not after you've fallen in. Fasten all buckles and adjust for snug fit.

Throw Preserver: Hold one end of the line, throw the ring past the victim (not at them), and pull the line to bring them in. Aim to land the ring beyond the victim so the rope crosses their body.
Why They're Needed
Water rescue is a significant risk in any district near bodies of water, flooding, or swimming pools. Swift water, cold water, and current all make drowning a real risk to rescuers as well as victims. The PFD doesn't make you a rescue swimmer — it keeps you alive if you fall in.
Also Known As
PFD, life jacket, life vest, floatie (informal). Ring buoy: life ring, throw ring, throw preserver, toss rope.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — REACH, THROW, ROW, GO
Water rescue follows a priority order: (1) Reach from shore, (2) Throw a line or ring, (3) Row or use a boat, (4) Go in as a last resort with a PFD. Do not enter swift or cold water without your department's water rescue training and proper equipment. More rescuers have drowned attempting water rescue than the original victims.
W-Tool (Hydraulic Spreading Tool)
What It Is
The W-Tool (also called a "battering ram" in battery-powered versions) is a hydraulic tool designed to spread door jambs — forcing space in the gap between a door and its frame. It can also be used as a battering ram to force doors. One end drives into the door gap; the W-shape applies spreading force to the jamb.
How to Use It
Insert the spreading ends into the door gap at the lock area. Activate the hydraulic mechanism to spread. Use in combination with the Halligan for stubborn doors, or alone where the Halligan won't seat properly. As a battery ram, swing it against the door for impact-based forced entry.
Why It's Needed
Some door configurations resist conventional irons technique — security doors, multiple-lock residential doors, commercial steel frames. The W-Tool provides a hydraulic option when manual technique isn't getting the job done.
Also Known As
W-tool, battering ram, door ram, hydraulic spreader, rabbit tool (Hurst brand), power entry tool.
Comp 5 Tool Box — Full Contents
What's Inside
Screwdrivers (various sizes), socket wrench + sockets, duct tape, box cutter, zip ties, tape measure, pipe wrench, hammer, Teflon tape, adjustable crescent wrench, small crowbar, wire cutters, window glazing tool, razor scraper, small sledgehammer, voltage tester, Allen key wrench set, pliers, punch, and 3 metric box wrenches (18mm + others).
Key Items to Know
Voltage Tester (starred in document): A non-contact or contact tester that indicates whether a conductor or surface is energized. Critical for any scene involving downed wires, electrical panels, or vehicle fires with compromised wiring. Never assume power is off without testing.

Window Glazing Tool: Used to remove window frames and glazing strips to extract window glass panels during rescue — quieter and more controlled than breaking.

Teflon Tape: PTFE thread tape used to seal threaded fittings — particularly hose connections with minor thread damage or leaks.

Punch: A hardened steel pin punch for driving out roll pins, starting holes, or breaching thin materials.
Why It's Needed
Extrication, rescue, and utility work require hand tools that hydraulic rescue tools can't do — precise work, small adjustments, and field repairs. This box covers scenarios from vehicle rescue to machinery entrapment to scene support.
⚠ VOLTAGE TESTER — CRITICAL AWARENESS
The document flags the voltage tester with multiple asterisks because it's easy to forget and catastrophic to need. Before touching any wire, panel, or component that could be energized — use the tester. Electricity on a fire or crash scene kills responders every year.
↑ Back to top
6

Compartment 6 — Water Rescue & Air Bottles

Officer's Side · Mustang Suit, Rope Throw, Carabiners, Air Bottles
Mustang Suit
What It Is
A marine-grade immersion suit (survival suit) that provides both thermal protection and buoyancy to a person in cold water. "Mustang" is a major manufacturer of marine immersion suits — the name has become genericized in many fire departments. These bright orange or red suits provide hypothermia protection for extended periods in cold water and keep the wearer afloat without effort.
How to Use It
  1. Sit down if possible while donning — these suits are bulky.
  2. Step both feet into the legs and pull the suit up over your turnout gear or uniform.
  3. Slide both arms in and zip the front closure fully.
  4. Secure the hood, wrist closures, and any remaining fasteners.
  5. The built-in buoyancy will keep you face-up in water even if unconscious.
Why It's Needed
Cold water kills through hypothermia and incapacitation within minutes. A firefighter who enters or falls into cold water without thermal protection loses fine motor control within 3–5 minutes and can lose consciousness within 30 minutes. The Mustang suit extends survival time dramatically for rescuers operating in or near cold water.
Also Known As
Mustang suit, immersion suit, survival suit, dry suit (though a true dry suit is different), floatation suit.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
The Mustang suit provides buoyancy but is not a substitute for training. If you are not trained in water rescue, do not enter the water — even suited up. Know the "Reach, Throw, Row, Go" priority order. Your suit keeps you alive if you go in accidentally; it doesn't make you a trained rescue swimmer.
Rope Throw Bag
What It Is
A bag pre-packed with a floating throw rope (typically 50–75 feet of ¼" polypropylene rope that floats). You throw the bag — not just the rope — to a victim in the water. The bag acts as a projectile and the rope pays out freely from the bag as it flies through the air.
How to Use It
  1. Open the bag top and confirm the rope is loaded and the free end is in your hand.
  2. Stand upstream of the victim in moving water.
  3. Swing the bag underhand and release — aim to land the bag just past the victim so the rope crosses them.
  4. Shout "ROPE!" as you throw — victim should grab the rope, not the bag.
  5. Brace yourself and let the victim pendulum to shore on the rope.
  6. To repack: stuff the rope back in the bag loosely — do not coil it, or it will tangle on the next throw.
Why It's Needed
Fastest water rescue tool available for a shore-based rescuer. A throw bag can reach a victim 50–70 feet away in 2 seconds. Compare that to any other option and the value is obvious.
Also Known As
Throw bag, rescue throw bag, rope bag, toss bag, Z-Rig bag (when configured for mechanical advantage).
Water Helmet
What It Is
A water rescue helmet — designed with ventilation, a low profile, and secure fastening for water entry and current navigation. Unlike a structural firefighting helmet, a water rescue helmet won't trap water and drag you under, and is designed to stay on in current.
Why It's Needed
Head protection during water rescue operations. Swift water currents drive rescuers into rocks, debris, bridge supports, and other structures. A water rescue helmet is the appropriate PPE for this environment — your structural helmet is not.
Also Known As
Water rescue helmet, swift water helmet, rescue helmet.
Life Safety Ring + Strap with 3 Carabiners
What They Are
Life Safety Ring: A rigid ring that fits around a victim's torso, keeping them at the surface and providing a grip point for rescuers.

Strap with 3 Carabiners: A rescue webbing strap with carabiner connectors for attaching the victim to a rescue system, or for building a simple mechanical advantage haul system or belayed water rescue.
Why They're Needed
Victim management in water rescue requires secure attachment. A panicked drowning victim will try to climb on top of a rescuer, potentially drowning both. The life ring keeps victim and rescuer at a managed distance. The carabiner strap connects victims to the rescue system for haul-out.
Also Known As
Life ring, life safety ring, rescue ring, cinch ring; the carabiner strap: rescue webbing, haul strap, rescue anchor.
Air Bottles ×4 — Under Compartment 6
What They Are
Four additional SCBA cylinders stored under Compartment 6. These supplement the 3 bottles stored outside Compartment 2 for a total of 7 spare bottles on the apparatus. Same as the bottles at Comp 2 — check pressure, check valve open status, every day.
Why It's Needed
Sustained interior operations at a working fire, multiple victim rescues, and prolonged searches all consume air. Seven spare bottles give the crew the ability to sustain air-intensive operations without waiting for re-supply.
Also Known As
Spare bottles, air cylinders, SCBA cylinders, spare air.
↑ Back to top
7

Compartment 7 — Fire Extinguishers & Spill Control

Officer's Side · All four extinguisher types + EV fire blanket
💡 THE FOUR CLASSES OF FIRE — REVIEW
Class A = Ordinary combustibles (wood, paper, fabric). Class B = Flammable liquids/gases. Class C = Electrical equipment (energized). Class D = Combustible metals. Class K = Cooking oils/fats. Know which extinguisher matches which class.
Silver Bullet — Pressurized Water Extinguisher
What It Is
A pressurized stainless steel cylinder (the "silver bullet" — named for its appearance) containing plain water under air pressure. Effective only on Class A fires (ordinary combustibles — wood, paper, fabric). No surfactant, no foam — just water.
How to Use It
Pull the pin, aim the nozzle at the base of the fire, squeeze the handle, and sweep side-to-side. Capacity is approximately 2.5 gallons — enough for a small Class A fire. Not a substitute for a hose line.
Why It's Needed
Small smoldering fires (trash can, weed fire at the base of a building) can be hit with the silver bullet without deploying a full hose line. Fast, clean, no secondary contamination, no residue.
Also Known As
Silver bullet, water can, pressurized water, 2½-gallon water can.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
Never use a water extinguisher on electrical fires (Class C) or flammable liquid fires (Class B). Water conducts electricity and will spread burning liquid fires. Know your agent and know your fire class.
ABC Dry Chemical Extinguisher
What It Is
A pressurized cylinder containing monoammonium phosphate (dry chemical powder). The "ABC" rating means it's effective on Class A (combustibles), Class B (flammable liquids), and Class C (energized electrical) fires. It suppresses fire by interrupting the chemical chain reaction.
How to Use It
PASS: Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, Sweep from side to side. Use in short bursts, starting from the near edge of the fire and sweeping through. Stay low, stay upwind.
Why It's Needed
Versatility. One extinguisher handles three classes. Ideal for vehicle fires, fuel-related fires, and any environment with multiple potential fire types. The most common extinguisher type you'll encounter.
Also Known As
ABC extinguisher, dry chem, dry chemical, monoammonium phosphate, the purple K (different dry chem specifically for Class B).
🔰 ROOKIE MISTAKE
Emptying the whole extinguisher in one shot and running out before the fire's knocked down. Use short controlled bursts. Dry chemical depletes fast and you can't reload on scene.
CO₂ Extinguisher
What It Is
A high-pressure cylinder of liquid carbon dioxide that converts to gas when discharged, smothering the fire by displacing oxygen and cooling the fuel. Effective on Class B (flammable liquids) and Class C (electrical) fires. Leaves no residue — critical for protecting sensitive electrical equipment and electronics.
How to Use It
PASS: Pull, Aim (hold the horn/nozzle — it will get extremely cold), Squeeze, Sweep. Keep distance — CO₂ discharges at -109°F and the horn can cause frostbite. Do not use in small enclosed spaces without ventilation — CO₂ depletes oxygen and can incapacitate rescuers.
Why It's Needed
Electrical panel fires, server rooms, electrical equipment fires. CO₂ leaves no residue and won't damage equipment the way dry chemical will. For any fire in or near sensitive electronics, CO₂ is the preferred agent.
Also Known As
CO₂ extinguisher, carbon dioxide extinguisher, the CO₂.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — FROSTBITE RISK
The discharge horn on a CO₂ extinguisher reaches -109°F. Never grab the horn bare-handed. Wear gloves. The cold gas discharge also looks alarming — fire is still present even as you're applying CO₂. Don't stop before the fire is confirmed out.
Class K Extinguisher
What It Is
A wet chemical extinguisher specifically designed for cooking oil and fat fires (Class K). Contains potassium acetate, potassium citrate, or potassium carbonate solutions that react with the cooking oil to form a soapy foam (saponification), effectively smothering the fire and preventing re-ignition.
How to Use It
Apply gently and from a distance — do not spray directly onto burning oil at close range, which can cause splashing and spread the fire. Move the nozzle side-to-side in a sweeping motion across the oil surface. Allow the foam blanket to form and smother.
Why It's Needed
Commercial kitchen fires are common and extremely dangerous. A deep fryer or commercial range fire at full temperature (400°F+) will re-ignite if you don't permanently lower the temperature of the oil below its auto-ignition point. Class K agents are specifically formulated to achieve this where ABC dry chemical or CO₂ fail to prevent re-ignition.
Also Known As
Class K, wet chemical, kitchen extinguisher, Ansul R-102 (common commercial suppression system brand).
Oil Dry
What It Is
A clay-based granular absorbent — used to soak up small petroleum product spills (fuel, oil, hydraulic fluid) on roadways or incident scenes. Sold under various brand names including Oil-Dri and Speedy Dry; in the firehouse it's most commonly called "oil dry," though some old-timers still call it "kitty litter."
How to Use It
Spread the granules over the spill, allow it to absorb the liquid (a few minutes), then sweep or shovel the saturated material into a bag or container for disposal. Temporary traction for slick roadway patches can also be created with dry application.
Why It's Needed
Vehicle accident scenes routinely produce fuel and fluid spills that create both fire risk and traffic hazard. Oil dry is the field-expedient solution for small spills without waiting for a hazmat team.
Also Known As
Oil dry, kitty litter, absorbent granules, floor dry, Oil-Dri (brand name), absorbent, Speedy Dry.
Fire Blanket — For Electric Vehicles
What It Is
A large, fire-resistant or fire-suppressing blanket specifically designed to be draped over a burning electric vehicle (EV). EV lithium-ion battery fires undergo "thermal runaway" — a self-sustaining chemical reaction that generates its own oxygen and cannot be extinguished with conventional water or dry chemical suppression. The blanket works by containing the heat and limiting oxygen to slow/halt the reaction, and by containing the fire to prevent spread to surrounding vehicles or structures.
How to Use It
  1. Ensure no occupants remain in the vehicle (or perform extraction before blanketing).
  2. Unfold the blanket and approach from upwind.
  3. Drape the blanket completely over the burning EV, covering as much surface as possible.
  4. Continue to monitor — EV thermal runaway can reignite or break through containment.
  5. Large volumes of cooling water into the battery compartment remain the primary suppression method; the blanket is a containment/spread-control tool.
Why It's Needed
EV fires are an emerging and growing challenge for the fire service. Lithium-ion battery thermal runaway can require 3,000+ gallons of water to suppress, can take hours to extinguish, and can reignite hours or days later. The blanket is a practical, field-deployable tool to contain the hazard and prevent fire spread while managing the incident.
Also Known As
EV fire blanket, electric vehicle blanket, battery fire blanket, thermal containment blanket.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — EV FIRES
Do not assume an EV fire is out just because flames are no longer visible. Thermal runaway can continue internally and reignite violently hours later. EV incidents require extended monitoring and documentation. Your turnout gear does NOT protect against the toxic gases (hydrogen fluoride, etc.) released in lithium-ion battery fires — stay upwind and in SCBA whenever working near burning EVs.
▶ WATCH IT IN ACTION
YouTube: "EV fire blanket electric vehicle fire suppression"
↑ Back to top
↑

Above the Compartments — Ladders & Pike Poles

Officer's Side Exterior · Extension Ladder 24 ft, Roof Ladder 14 ft, Pike Poles 6 & 8 ft
Extension Ladder 24 ft + Roof Ladder 14 ft
What They Are
Extension Ladder (24 ft): A two-section aluminum extension ladder. At 24 feet of working length, it reaches second and some third-story windows — your primary egress/rescue ladder for residential structures.

Roof Ladder (14 ft): A 14-foot single-section ladder with hinged hooks at the top. The hooks are deployed at the ridge of a pitched roof so the ladder lays flat against the roof surface and stays put while a firefighter walks the rungs to work on the roof.
How to Use Them
  1. Carry to the target, heel the butt of the ladder against the wall base.
  2. Set ladder angle at approximately 75 degrees (1 foot out for every 4 feet of height — the "1-in-4" rule).
  3. For rescue ladders: tip should extend 2–3 rungs above the window sill.
  4. For roof access: tip should extend 3–5 rungs above the roofline.
  5. Confirm the ladder is seated on solid ground — not on a soft surface, slope, or ice.
  6. Never stand on the top two rungs of any ladder.
Why They're Needed
Victim rescue from upper floors, secondary egress for trapped crews, roof access for ventilation, and any operation above the first floor where ground or apparatus access isn't available. Ground ladders save lives — know how to throw them fast and correctly.
Also Known As
Extension ladder, ext ladder, 24-footer; roof ladder, hook ladder, 14-footer.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — LADDER PLACEMENT FOR RESCUE
When placing a ladder for victim rescue at a window, always place the tip of the ladder to the side of the window opening, not in front of it. A victim jumping before you reach the window will hit the ladder. Place the ladder with the tip beside the window frame — much safer for both of you.
▶ WATCH IT IN ACTION
YouTube: "fire service ground ladder throw and raise"
Pike Poles ×2 — 6 ft & 8 ft (Above Compartments)
What They Are
Long-handled tools with a sharpened steel point and hook at the top. Used for pulling, pushing, and probing materials at distance — specifically: pulling down burning ceiling materials, probing for fire in walls, moving burning debris, and clearing overhaul areas. The 6-foot and 8-foot lengths (plus the 4-6 ft closet pike in Comp 2) give you options for any ceiling height.
How to Use Them
Use the point to punch into ceiling surfaces; use the hook to pull materials down and away. Work in a systematic pattern during overhaul — open the ceiling to reveal the full extent of fire travel above the ceiling plane. Keep your face mask on — opened ceiling cavities often contain superheated smoke and gas that release suddenly.
Why They're Needed
Overhaul and ventilation. You cannot see fire in a wall or ceiling until you open it. Pike poles let you do this efficiently from floor level without climbing or risk of contact with falling material.
Also Known As
Pike pole, hook, ceiling hook, plaster hook, overhaul hook, pull hook, 6-footer, 8-footer.
↑ Back to top
C

Inside the Cab

EMS Bags, Gas Meters, AED, Radios, Accountability, ERG
TOP SHELF
4-Gas CO Meter (O₂, CO, H₂S, Combustible Gas)
What It Is
A four-sensor electronic atmospheric monitor that simultaneously detects and measures: Oxygen (O₂) level, Carbon Monoxide (CO), Hydrogen Sulfide (H₂S), and combustible/flammable gas (typically measured as LEL — Lower Explosive Limit percentage). This is your primary atmospheric testing tool before and during entry into potentially hazardous atmospheres.
How to Use It
  1. Turn on and allow to calibrate in fresh air — do not start in a contaminated atmosphere.
  2. Test the atmosphere BEFORE entry — poke the sampling probe through a keyhole, gap, or small opening first.
  3. Normal readings: O₂ 20.9%, CO 0 ppm, H₂S 0 ppm, LEL 0%.
  4. Alarm thresholds: CO >35 ppm (TWA), O₂ <19.5% or >23.5%, H₂S >10 ppm, LEL >10%.
  5. Never bypass or ignore alarms — the meter detects what your senses cannot.
Why It's Needed
CO is odorless and colorless. H₂S smells like rotten eggs at low levels but paralyzes your sense of smell at higher concentrations. Oxygen deficiency causes rapid incapacitation without warning. Combustible gas at 10% LEL is 10% of the way to an explosion. The meter detects all of these — your nose and eyes do not.
Also Known As
4-gas meter, multi-gas meter, CGI (combustible gas indicator), MSA (brand name), RAE meter, atmospheric tester, gas monitor.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
Always bump-test your meter before every shift. A bump test (brief exposure to a known test gas concentration) confirms all four sensors are working. A meter that hasn't been bump-tested may show clean readings in a contaminated atmosphere and kill you. This is not optional.
Gas Trac (Methane Meter)
What It Is
The Gas Trac — a dedicated combustible gas detector optimized for natural gas (methane / CH₄) detection. Used for gas-leak investigations, suspected gas alarms, and confined-space air monitoring before entry.
How to Use It
For gas investigations: sweep the meter through the space and watch the combustible gas percentage. Check low (some fuel gases are heavier than air) and high (methane is lighter — it accumulates near the ceiling). Bump-test before every shift.
Why It's Needed
Natural-gas leaks are a routine call type and a serious explosion risk. The Gas Trac quantifies the hazard — telling you not just that gas is present but at what percent of LEL — so you know whether to evacuate, shut utilities, or stand down.
Also Known As
Gas Trac, gas tracker, methane meter, combustible gas indicator. NOT the HCN sensor — that is a separate device.
HCN Sensor (Standalone)
What It Is
A dedicated standalone Hydrogen Cyanide (HCN) sensor — a separate device from the Gas Trac. HCN is produced in almost every structural fire from burning synthetics, foam, and plastics. It is one of the primary killers in smoke inhalation — more dangerous than CO in many fire scenarios.
How to Use It
During and after a structure fire: sweep the sensor through the work area, monitor the HCN reading. Use it during overhaul to confirm SCBA is still required (it almost always is) and to inform any decisions about removing masks. Bump-test on the same schedule as the 4-gas and Gas Trac.
Why It's Needed
HCN is a fire-service silent killer. Modern building contents — foam furniture, synthetic carpets, plastics, composite materials — all off-gas hydrogen cyanide when they burn. The 4-gas meter does not have an HCN sensor; the Gas Trac on this rig is for methane only. The standalone HCN sensor fills that gap.
Also Known As
HCN sensor, HCN meter, hydrogen cyanide detector, cyanide meter. Distinct from the Gas Trac.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — HCN AWARENESS
HCN has an IDLH (Immediately Dangerous to Life and Health) of just 50 ppm. Smoke from a typical house fire can contain 50–300 ppm of HCN. This is why you never, ever take your mask off inside a fire building or during active overhaul — even when flames are out, HCN and other toxins remain.
Hot Stick
What It Is
A non-contact voltage detector on a long insulated pole — essentially a voltage sensor mounted on a fiberglass extension stick. When held near energized conductors or electrical components, it buzzes or lights up to indicate voltage presence without requiring physical contact.
How to Use It
Extend the hot stick toward the suspected conductor or electrical component from a safe distance. If the meter activates (light, buzz, alarm), the object is energized — do not touch, do not get closer, notify your officer, and request utility company response.
Why It's Needed
Downed power lines, vehicle accidents involving utility poles, and fires near electrical infrastructure are extremely hazardous. The hot stick lets you test electrical status from a safe distance before committing personnel to the immediate hazard area.
Also Known As
Hot stick, voltage detector, tic tracer, non-contact voltage tester, sonar stick, electrical tester.
Blue Lockout / Tagout Bag
What It Is
A bag containing lockout/tagout (LOTO) equipment — padlocks, hasps, locking devices, and warning tags used to physically lock out energy sources (electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic) during rescue operations at machinery or industrial incidents. Prevents a machine from being re-energized while someone is working on or near it.
Why It's Needed
Industrial and machinery entrapment rescues require positive control of energy sources. OSHA's LOTO standard (29 CFR 1910.147) exists because uncontrolled re-energization of machinery causes catastrophic injuries. When you're reaching into a machine to free a victim's hand, that machine must be positively locked off.
Also Known As
LOTO bag, lockout tagout kit, energy control bag.
MIDDLE SHELF — EMS BAGS
Red Jump Bag — "First In" EMS Bag
What It Is
The primary emergency medical bag — the first bag taken to a patient. Contains the initial assessment and life-threat treatment supplies: airway adjuncts, oxygen masks, non-rebreather mask, blood pressure cuff, stethoscope, gloves, trauma dressings, tourniquets, pulse ox, and basic cardiac monitoring supplies. The exact contents vary by department protocol — know your bag's exact contents.
Why It's Needed
The first minutes of a medical emergency are the most critical. This bag is pre-packed, pre-organized, and designed for rapid deployment on any EMS call. You grab it and go — no sorting, no hunting.
Also Known As
Jump bag, first-in bag, ALS bag, BLS bag, medic bag, go bag, the red bag.
Green Airway Bag
What It Is
A dedicated bag for airway management supplies — contains equipment for securing and maintaining a patient's airway. Typically includes: BVM (bag-valve-mask) resuscitator, oral and nasal airway adjuncts (OPA/NPA), suction bulb or device, end-tidal CO₂ monitoring supplies, supraglottic airway devices (King LT, iGel), intubation supplies if ALS-level, and oxygen delivery equipment.
Why It's Needed
Airway is the "A" in the ABCs of emergency medicine for a reason — it comes first. Without an open airway, nothing else matters. Having a dedicated bag means airway equipment is always organized, accessible, and complete.
Also Known As
Airway bag, green bag, intubation bag, respiratory bag, ventilation bag.
AED — Automated External Defibrillator
What It Is
A computerized device that analyzes a cardiac patient's heart rhythm, determines if a shockable rhythm (ventricular fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia) is present, and delivers a controlled electrical shock to attempt to restore a normal rhythm. The AED talks you through the process — it literally tells you what to do.
How to Use It
  1. Power on the AED — it will begin verbal instructions immediately.
  2. Apply pads as shown in the diagram: one below the right collarbone, one on the left lateral chest wall below the armpit.
  3. Ensure all personnel are clear of the patient — shout "CLEAR!"
  4. Follow the AED's instructions for shock delivery or continued CPR.
  5. Resume high-quality CPR immediately after the shock — do not wait to check for a pulse.
Why It's Needed
Early defibrillation is one of the highest-impact interventions in cardiac arrest. For every minute of VF without defibrillation, survival decreases 7–10%. As the first arriving unit, your AED may arrive before ALS — it saves lives when used immediately.
Also Known As
AED, defibrillator, defib, cardiac monitor (when a full 12-lead monitor is carried), the AED.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
Do not touch the patient during AED rhythm analysis or shock delivery. Ensure all personnel are visually confirmed clear before the shock. Post-shock, immediately resume CPR — do not interrupt compressions to check for a pulse until the AED or your officer instructs otherwise.
Small Orange Bag — Suction Device
What It Is
A portable suction device — manual (squeeze/bulb-type) or battery-powered — used to clear a patient's airway of blood, vomit, fluids, and secretions. Without suction, a compromised airway filled with fluid cannot be managed by BVM or any other airway device.
How to Use It
Attach the appropriate suction tip (rigid Yankauer or flexible catheter), turn on or activate the device, and suction the visible airway using sweeping motions. Do not suction for more than 10 seconds at a time — you're also removing oxygen. Suction, then ventilate.
Why It's Needed
Vomiting during resuscitation is common — especially during CPR and BVM ventilation. Without suction, vomit enters the lungs and causes aspiration pneumonia and airway obstruction. Suction is non-negotiable for any unconscious or compromised patient.
Also Known As
Suction, suction device, portable suction, V-VAC, SSCOR, manual suction, the orange bag (suction).
Pet O₂ Mask
What It Is
A set of oxygen masks sized for dogs, cats, and other small animals — typically a set of three sizes (small, medium, large) designed to fit over animal snouts and muzzles. Connected to standard oxygen supply equipment.
Why It's Needed
Animals — especially pets rescued from house fires — suffer smoke inhalation just like humans. Providing supplemental oxygen to a compromised animal buys time for veterinary care and often saves animals that would otherwise die from smoke inhalation. It's also a community relations and public trust tool — people care deeply about their pets.
Also Known As
Pet O₂ mask, animal oxygen mask, pet resuscitator, Wallis mask (trade name).
ALSO IN CAB — KEY ITEMS
ERG — Emergency Response Guidebook
What It Is
The Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG), published by the US Department of Transportation, is a pocket reference for first responders at hazardous materials incidents. Organized by UN/NA chemical placard number or chemical name, it provides: initial isolation distances, protective action distances, recommended PPE level, fire response guidance, spill response guidance, and first aid information for hundreds of hazardous chemicals.
How to Use It
  1. Read the placard on the vehicle or container — find the four-digit UN/NA number.
  2. Look up the number in the orange (or yellow/blue) section — find the Guide Number.
  3. Turn to that Guide page for response guidance.
  4. For certain highlighted materials, also check the Green Section for specific initial isolation and protective action distances.
Why It's Needed
On a hazmat incident, you're making life-safety decisions about isolation, evacuation, and approach with very little time and often no on-scene hazmat specialist. The ERG is your first-response reference. It could keep you from walking into a chlorine cloud, an explosive atmosphere, or a radioactive spill without knowing it.
Also Known As
ERG, Emergency Response Guidebook, DOT guidebook, hazmat guide, the orange book (for the orange-covered edition).
▶ WATCH IT IN ACTION
YouTube: "how to use the ERG Emergency Response Guidebook"
KnoxBox + Elevator Key
What They Are
KnoxBox Key: A master key to Knox-brand rapid entry key boxes mounted on commercial buildings. Building owners secure their keys inside these tamper-resistant boxes; the fire department holds the single master key on each apparatus. On a fire or alarm call, you use this key to open the Knox box and retrieve the building key — no forced entry required.

Elevator Key: A "fire service key" (often a triangular key or specific brand key) that allows firefighters to take manual control of elevator cars — stopping them at a specific floor, holding doors open, and using the elevator for personnel and equipment transport.
Why They're Needed
Knox boxes eliminate the need for forced entry at commercial structures on the vast majority of alarm responses. This saves thousands of dollars in damaged doors and saves time on every response. Elevator keys are critical for high-rise operations where elevators are the only practical vertical transport option.
Also Known As
Knox key, rapid entry key, Knox system; elevator key: fire service key, elevator master key, recall key.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY — ELEVATOR USE IN FIRES
Never use an elevator for evacuation in a fire. Use the elevator for firefighter equipment transport only, after positive confirmation that the floor the elevator services is not the fire floor. An elevator that opens on the fire floor can strand a crew in a smoke-filled shaft with no exit.
Accountability Velcro Name Board
What It Is
A velcro board or passport system used to track crew accountability at an incident. Each firefighter has a passport (a velcro card with their name and assignment). When entering the hazard zone, passports are left with the entry control officer. The board gives the IC and accountability officer a real-time picture of who is inside and who is outside.
How to Use It
On arrival, remove your passport from your helmet or the apparatus board. Hand it to the entry control/accountability officer when entering the structure. Retrieve it when exiting. The board should always reflect who is currently inside the hazard zone.
Why It's Needed
If a MAYDAY is declared or a structural collapse occurs, the IC must know who is inside, what their assignment was, and where they were working. Accountability is how you recover a downed firefighter. Without it, you're searching blind in a building you can't safely enter.
Also Known As
Accountability board, passport system, PASSPORT, velcro board, NIMS accountability system.
⚠ CRITICAL SAFETY
Accountability is a culture, not just a tool. If your department uses a passport system, using it is non-negotiable on every entry. One firefighter who bypasses accountability on the day there's a MAYDAY is one firefighter who may not get found in time. Use the system. Every time.
↑ Back to top
T

Top of the Engine

Snow Shovel, Traffic Cones, Fire Paddle, Manifold, Dawn Soap

Top-of-Engine Equipment

  • Snow Shovel: For clearing snow from hydrant caps and access paths in winter. Always know where your hydrants are in snow — buried hydrants add precious minutes to water supply operations. Your district has them; know them.
  • 1" Garden Hose: Secondary utility hose stored on top for quick access. Same use as the one in the Engineer's compartment.
  • Traffic Cones: Scene perimeter and traffic management on road incidents. Place them immediately on arrival at any roadway incident — your rig protects you; cones extend that protection zone. Never underestimate traffic.
  • Fire Paddle: A flat paddle-style tool for patting out or smothering small ground fires — brush fires, grass fires, small flare-ups. Swatting/paddling beats a hose line for small spot fires in open terrain. Also called a Fire Swatter, flap, or beater.
  • Manifold for Fire Gun / Deck Gun: The supply manifold for the deck gun (master stream mounted on top of the apparatus). Multiple inlets allow multiple supply lines to feed the deck gun for maximum flow. This is your defensive exterior master stream — flows 500–1000+ GPM.
  • Dawn Soap and Brush in Bucket: For cleaning hose, equipment, and the apparatus itself. Also used as a foam additive for certain wetting applications on Class A materials (though Class A foam concentrate is preferred). The bucket and brush are the end-of-shift cleanup kit.
⚠ DECK GUN / MASTER STREAM SAFETY
When the deck gun is flowing, no one enters the building. Master streams are a defensive operation. The pressure and flow a master stream delivers will injure firefighters inside, cause structural compromise, and reduce steam-burn survivability. When the deck gun goes to work, interior crews come out. No exceptions.
↑ Back to top
≠

E62 vs. E61 — Key Differences

Know the differences — you may ride either rig
🚒 KNOW YOUR RIG
Both engines share most of their tool placement, but these differences matter on the fireground.

Differences at a Glance

  • Driver's Side Over Wheel — E62: Air bags stored here. E61: Pry axe (officer's tool) stored here instead.
  • Air Bag Location — E61: Stored in the compartment near the back on the driver's side (not over the wheel). E62: Over the wheel and in Comp 3.
  • Air Bag Controllers: Both engines have different controllers. Both systems inflate to 118 PSI maximum. Do not assume the controller is the same — verify which you're on before operating.
  • RIT Pack: E62 has it — top shelf of Comp 3. E61 does not — plan accordingly on RIT assignments.
  • Officer Side Rear — E61: Contains a crowbar, 2 shovels (spade and flat), and a Pig. E62: These items are not in that location.
  • Officer Side Middle — E61: Has ice cleats for boot bottoms. E62 does not.
  • Toolbox — E61: Contains a hacksaw. E62 toolbox does not.
🔰 ROOKIE MISTAKE — "SAME RIG" ASSUMPTION
Cross-trained firefighters who know E62 cold have been caught flat-footed reaching for air bags over the wheel on E61 and finding an officer's tool instead. Before every shift, confirm which engine you're riding and verify the differences. A 30-second orientation on the ramp is worth 30 seconds of confusion at an incident.
↑ Back to top

A final word from your instructor: A compartment check isn't a chore — it's your daily handshake with the rig. When you're crawling blind in a smoke-filled hallway at 3am, you won't be thinking about this guide. You'll be operating on muscle memory built during a thousand quiet moments of knowing exactly where everything lives. Build that muscle memory now, while you have time. Pick up every fitting. Say its name. Know what it does. Know why it's there. That's what makes a firefighter.

Stay low. Stay together. Stay safe.
