📚 Utility 61 — Compartment Study Guide

Utility 61 is the department's multi-purpose support vehicle — water rescue capability, technical rescue tools, scene support, and hazmat initial response all in one platform. Know every bag, every bin, and every tool before you ride it.

📋 Click Here for more details and photos of Utility 61

📻

Front Dash — Communications

DuCom · Fireground radio · PA system
DASH-01
DuCom (Gray Microphone)
AKA: DuCom, dispatch radio, main radio, county radio
+
📖What it is

A gray push-to-talk microphone connected to the DuPage County interoperable communications (DuCom) radio system. This is the primary channel for dispatch communication — the mic you key up to contact dispatch for assignments, updates, scene reports, and resource requests.

❓Why it's needed

Dispatch communication is your lifeline. Every assignment, address change, resource request, and scene update runs through DuCom. Losing contact with dispatch on a working incident is a significant safety problem.

🔧How to use
  1. Know which channel is assigned for your district before the call.
  2. Press and hold the PTT (push-to-talk) button.
  3. Wait 1 second after pressing before speaking — gives the repeater time to key up.
  4. Speak clearly: unit ID → message. Example: "Utility 61 to DuCom..."
  5. Release and wait for response.
  6. Never talk over another unit — listen first.
⚠️
Wait 1 Second Before SpeakingKeying and immediately talking clips the first word. The repeater needs a moment to key up. "Utility 61" becomes "tility 61" and now dispatch is asking you to repeat. Pause — then speak.
💡
Gray = County, Black Left = FiregroundThree mics, three channels. Gray is for county/dispatch. Don't mix them up on scene.
DASH-02
Fireground Microphone (Black — Lower Left)
AKA: Tac mic, tactical channel mic, fireground radio
+
📖What it is

The black push-to-talk microphone at the lower left of the dash, connected to the fireground (tactical) channel. Used for crew-to-crew communication at a working incident — coordinating with attack crews, command, and other apparatus on scene.

🔧How to use
  1. Confirm you're on the correct tac channel for the incident before transmitting.
  2. PTT, wait 1 second, speak: unit/location → message.
  3. Keep transmissions short and specific.
  4. Critical messages get three words first: Mayday, Emergency, or Emergency Traffic.
❓Why it's needed

Fireground communication is separated from dispatch to avoid cluttering the county channel during operations. Command and crews talk on tac; dispatch stays on DuCom.

⚠️
Mayday ProtocolIf a firefighter is lost, trapped, or injured: LOUD — "Mayday, Mayday, Mayday, [name], [company], [location], [situation]." Do not hesitate. Do not minimize. Key up and transmit.
DASH-03
PA System Microphone (Black — Upper Right)
AKA: PA, public address, exterior speaker
+
📖What it is

The black microphone at the upper right connected to the external public address speaker on the vehicle. Broadcasts your voice to people outside the apparatus without opening a window.

❓Why it's needed

Scene control at roadway incidents — directing bystanders, alerting pedestrians, instructing people to clear an area. Also useful for directing traffic around a scene or providing information to waiting family members outside a structure.

💡
Great for Traffic ControlAt MVAs or roadway incidents, the PA beats rolling down a window and shouting. You control volume, you're audible over engine noise, and you keep both hands free.
🗂️

Glove Compartment

Maps · ERG · Flares · Passport · Accountability
GLV-01
Maps — District Street Maps
AKA: Street atlas, paper nav, district maps, A-to-Z
+
📖What it is

Physical paper street maps of the response district. Your no-battery, no-signal, no-crash backup navigation system. Still works when the MDT freezes, GPS drops signal, or a crew member's phone is dead.

🔧How to use
  1. Know how to fold it open to your district before you need it.
  2. Orient to your direction of travel — north isn't always at the top of a folded map.
  3. Cross-reference nearest intersection to address for fastest routing.
  4. Know your district's major arteries cold so the map is confirmation, not discovery.
⚠️
Don't Rely on Technology AloneMDTs crash, GPS glitches, and cell service drops in rural or underground environments. The crew that can navigate by paper map is the one that still arrives on time when technology fails.
GLV-02
Truck Loading Instruction Paper
AKA: Load chart, weight distribution sheet, apparatus loading guide
+
📖What it is

A reference document specifying how equipment should be loaded on Utility 61 — proper weight distribution, tie-down requirements, and equipment placement to maintain safe handling.

❓Why it's needed

Improperly loaded utility vehicles handle poorly and can tip in emergency evasive maneuvers. After pulling gear at an incident, equipment gets thrown back in haste. This document tells you the correct placement so the rig handles the same way going home as it did going to the call.

GLV-03
Patient Prepare Reports (Blank)
AKA: PCR, patient care reports, run reports, medical forms
+
📖What it is

Blank paper patient care reporting forms for documenting medical incidents — patient demographics, chief complaint, vitals, interventions, and crew information.

🔧How to use
  1. Name, DOB, address, chief complaint.
  2. Vitals with timestamps (BP, pulse, resp, SpO2) — initial and trending.
  3. Interventions applied with times.
  4. Crew names and ID numbers.
  5. Legible — this is a legal document.
⚠️
Legibility Is a Legal RequirementPatient care reports are legal documents and medical records. Illegible handwriting can result in disciplinary action and creates liability if a medical error occurs. Take 30 seconds to write clearly.
GLV-04
Vehicle Name Laminate
AKA: Rig ID tag, apparatus card, unit identifier
+
📖What it is

A laminated card identifying this vehicle as "Utility 61." Used for staging identification, Passport accountability, and ensuring mutual aid or unfamiliar crews can correctly identify the apparatus.

❓Why it's needed

At a multi-unit incident with mutual aid, visual identification prevents radio confusion. The laminate is also used in the Passport accountability system to track which unit is on scene.

GLV-05
Spare Tire Lock Key (In Bag)
AKA: Spare tire key, lug lock key, anti-theft key
+
📖What it is

A specialized key required to unlock the security lug nut on the spare tire mount. Without this key, the spare tire cannot be removed — even if you have a jack and lug wrench.

❓Why it's needed

A flat tire on a utility vehicle carrying equipment is an out-of-service situation. The spare tire lock prevents theft but creates a failure point — this key is the only way to access the spare.

⚠️
Know Where This Key Is Before You Have a FlatA roadside tire change in the dark with equipment to transport is already stressful. Hunting for the spare key on top of that is avoidable. Know it's in a bag in the glove compartment before you need it.
GLV-06
Road Flares (×2)
AKA: Highway flares, fusees, emergency flares, road signals
+
📖What it is

Two pyrotechnic road flares — burning for 15–30 minutes and visible from over a mile. Used to warn approaching traffic of a hazard ahead.

🔧How to use
  1. Remove the cap.
  2. Strike the friction cap against the striking surface — like a large match.
  3. Hold away from your body when lighting — the initial flare is intense.
  4. Place in the roadway at intervals before the scene (e.g., 100 ft, 200 ft, 300 ft back) — not alongside it.
  5. Never place near fuel spills, leaking vehicles, or flammable liquid hazards.
⚠️
Never Near Fuel SpillsA burning flare near a fuel leak from a wrecked vehicle = ignition source. At any MVA with fuel leakage or smell of gas, do NOT light flares. Use LED warning devices instead.
💡
Traffic Behind You is Trying to Kill YouThe statistics are clear: struck-by-vehicle is a leading LODD cause. Place flares FAR back — at least 300 feet on a 50 mph road. Make the driver slow down before they can even see your apparatus.
GLV-07
Passport Accountability System
AKA: Passport, accountability tags, name tags, velcro tags, ICS accountability
+
📖What it is

A physical accountability system using velcro name tags. Each firefighter's name tag attaches to the Passport. The driver places names upside down on the Passport. The white velcro Passport goes to the Incident Commander. The red velcro Passport stays with the vehicle. This gives command a real-time physical record of every crew member assigned to the incident.

🔧How to use
  1. Collect name tags from crew members boarding Utility 61.
  2. Place tags upside down on the Passport board.
  3. White Passport → to Incident Commander or Accountability Officer on arrival.
  4. Red Passport → stays with the vehicle.
  5. When crew members leave the scene or reassign, update the Passport immediately.
⚠️
Upside-Down Tags Is the System — Not a MistakeTags go on upside down deliberately so they must be deliberately flipped over to be read. This small friction prevents accidental removal and signals that the person is actively assigned, not just passing through.
✅
Your Name Tag On = You're AccountableNo name tag on the Passport = command doesn't know you're on scene. In a Mayday, that's the difference between an immediate search and a delayed one.
▶ Watch: Passport Accountability System
GLV-08
Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)
AKA: ERG, orange book, hazmat book, DOT guidebook
+
📖What it is

The U.S. DOT Emergency Response Guidebook — the orange/yellow book used for initial hazmat incident response. Contains: Yellow pages (4-digit UN/NA numbers in numerical order → guide number); Blue pages (material names alphabetical → guide number); Orange pages (response guides: hazards, PPE, evacuation, first aid, spill control); Green pages (initial evacuation/shelter-in-place distances for toxic inhalation hazards; over 50 gal = large spill with extended distances). Back pages contain emergency phone numbers including CHEMTREC (1-800-424-9300).

🔧How to use
  1. Identify the material — read the placard number or name.
  2. Yellow pages: look up the 4-digit UN/NA number → note the guide number.
  3. Blue pages: look up by name if no number visible.
  4. Turn to that guide number in the Orange pages → hazards, PPE, initial response actions.
  5. If material is highlighted in Green in yellow/blue → also check Green pages for evacuation distances.
  6. For toxic gas threats: Green pages → find spill size (small/large) → day or night → distance.
⚠️
Green Highlighting = Toxic Inhalation or Water ReactiveMaterials highlighted green in the yellow or blue sections are either toxic inhalation hazards OR water-reactive materials that produce toxic gas on contact with water. These get special attention in the Green pages and have evacuation zones, not just safety distances.
💡
UN vs NA NumbersUN numbers are international (UN1203 = gasoline worldwide). NA numbers are North America-specific — used for materials regulated domestically but not assigned an international UN number. Both are four digits and work the same way in the ERG.
▶ Watch: How to Use the ERG
🦺

Door Pockets — Driver + Officer

Roadway vests × 2
DOOR-01
Roadway Safety Vest (×2 — One Per Door)
AKA: Hi-vis vest, ANSI vest, traffic vest, road vest, reflective vest
+
📖What it is

ANSI Class II or III high-visibility reflective safety vests — one in the driver's door pocket, one in the officer door pocket. Neon yellow-green or orange with retroreflective silver tape. Makes the wearer visible to approaching drivers day and night.

❓Why it's needed

NFPA 1500 and OSHA 1926.201 require high-visibility PPE at roadway incidents. Firefighter PPE (turnouts) is not a substitute — turnout gear retroreflective tape is designed for fire conditions, not traffic visibility. A hi-vis vest is mandatory at any roadway incident.

🔧How to use
  1. Put it on before stepping out of the apparatus at any roadway incident.
  2. Zip or snap closed — a vest blowing open in passing traffic doesn't protect you.
  3. Wear OVER turnout coat if gear is being worn.
  4. Do not store or stuff in a way that damages the retroreflective tape — damaged tape doesn't reflect at night.
⚠️
Vest On Before Feet Hit the GroundThe most dangerous moment at a roadway incident is getting out of the apparatus into live traffic. Vest goes on while you're still inside — not after you've stepped out. The two seconds it takes to don the vest could be the two seconds a distracted driver needs to react.
💺

Front Bench + Back Seat

PPE · Radios
SEAT-01
PPE — Personal Protective Equipment (Back Seat)
AKA: Gear, turnouts, bunker gear, structural firefighting PPE
+
📖What it is

Full structural firefighting PPE stored in the back seat, readily accessible to crew members boarding Utility 61. Includes turnout coat and pants (bunker gear), helmet, gloves, hood, and SCBA face piece if applicable.

🔧How to use
  1. Don pants first — step in, pull up, clip/snap the closures.
  2. Don coat — zip and snap ALL closures including collar.
  3. SCBA hood under helmet, helmet secured.
  4. Gloves last — until they are needed (keeps dexterity for rigging, driving).
  5. 30 seconds or less is the expectation.
❓Why it's needed

PPE in the crew cab means crew can be donning gear en route — arriving dressed and ready rather than gearing up on scene while the fire grows. Every second in turnouts is a second not wasted.

⚠️
ALL Closures Must Be Closed — All of ThemAn unzipped collar or unsnapped chest can cause a serious burn from radiant heat in seconds. Inspect every snap, every zipper, every closure before crossing the threshold.
SEAT-02
Portable Radios (×4)
AKA: Portables, handie-talkies, HTs, walkie-talkies
+
📖What it is

Four portable two-way radios stored in the back seat, ensuring every crew member has independent radio capability when not in direct contact with the apparatus.

🔧How to use
  1. Check battery level before every shift — at least two bars.
  2. Confirm correct channel assignment for the incident.
  3. Clip to turnout coat chest strap or use radio strap — secured, not loose.
  4. When transmitting: PTT → wait 1 second → identify → message.
  5. Keep radio out of water and away from extreme heat (inside burning structure).
❓Why it's needed

Individual radio capability means every crew member can hear incident updates, receive a Mayday, transmit an emergency, and stay connected even if separated from the apparatus.

⚠️
Dead Battery = Lost ContactA portable with a dead battery is just a brick. Check charge every single shift. On a multi-hour incident, a starting charge of 40% won't last.
📦

Truck Bed — Cases and Bins

MSA case · Milk crate · Gray bin · Water rescue · Rope
BED-01
MSA Case — SCBA + Air Bottle + Face Piece (Size M)
AKA: MSA case, breathing apparatus case, self-contained breathing apparatus
+
📖What it is

An MSA (Mine Safety Appliances) hard case containing a complete SCBA unit: an air cylinder, the SCBA harness and regulator, and a size Medium face piece. Provides respiratory protection in IDLH (Immediately Dangerous to Life and Health) atmospheres.

🔧How to use
  1. Don harness — shoulder straps first, waist belt cinched.
  2. Connect cylinder valve — open slowly counterclockwise.
  3. Don face piece — pull straps bottom to top for even seal.
  4. Inhale once to seat the regulator, confirm airflow.
  5. Confirm PASS device is armed.
  6. Check cylinder pressure before entering — 4,500 psi = full.
❓Why it's needed

Utility 61 may respond to hazmat incidents, confined space situations, or structural fires where respiratory protection is needed. Having a complete SCBA means the crew has entry capability without waiting for engine resources.

⚠️
Size M Only — Seal MattersThe face piece in this case is size M. If that's not your fit, you need a different face piece — a poor seal means contaminated air enters around the mask. Maintain fit test records.
▶ Watch: SCBA Donning Procedure
BED-02
Milk Crate — Contents
AKA: Utility crate, supply crate
+
🔧Contents
  • Jumper cables — 20-25 ft, heavy gauge for vehicle jump-starts
  • Wheel chocks — blocks placed at vehicle tires to prevent rolling at incidents
  • Caution tape — yellow perimeter tape for scene control
  • Receiver and hitch ball — tow attachment hardware for trailer or recovery operations
🔧Jumper Cables — How to Use
  1. Dead battery: Red (+) to dead battery (+) → Red (+) to good battery (+) → Black (-) to good battery (-) → Black (-) to engine block/chassis ground on dead vehicle (NOT dead battery negative).
  2. Start good vehicle, let run 2 minutes.
  3. Start dead vehicle.
  4. Remove in reverse order.
⚠️
Negative Goes to Chassis — Not Dead BatteryConnecting the negative to the dead battery terminal creates a spark risk near the hydrogen gas venting from the battery. Connect to an unpainted metal chassis point instead.
✅
Wheel Chocks Before You Get Under — Or Near — A VehicleAt any vehicle incident, place wheel chocks before working under or near the vehicle. A vehicle in gear can roll unexpectedly, especially if damaged. Chocks are non-negotiable in any rescue situation.
BED-03
Gray Bin — Water Rescue Equipment
AKA: Water rescue bin, swift water gear
+
🔧Contents
  • 4 Waders — chest or hip waders for shallow-water rescue and bank operations
  • 14" Inner tube — flotation device for victim reach/throw assist
  • 100 lb Lift Bag — pressurized airbag for lifting submerged or trapped items up to 100 lbs
  • 250 lb Lift Bag — pressurized airbag for heavier underwater recovery up to 250 lbs
  • PFD (Personal Flotation Device) — life jacket for rescuer water entry
🔧Lift Bags — How to Use
  1. Identify the lift point — attach bag under, around, or against the object.
  2. Connect air supply (low-pressure input from SCBA or dedicated inflator).
  3. Inflate slowly — watch for object shift or roll.
  4. Use a safety line in addition to the lift bag — a burst bag drops the load instantly.
  5. 100 lb bag: smaller submerged items, equipment recovery.
  6. 250 lb bag: larger submerged items, vehicle recovery support.
⚠️
Lift Bags Are NOT for Human RescueLift bags provide unpredictable, rapid lift. Using one attached to a person creates catastrophic injury risk. They recover objects, not people.
⚠️
Waders + Moving Water = TrappedWaders fill with water if you fall in moving current and become a deadly anchor. In any water deeper than knee height or with significant flow, waders are NOT the right PPE. Swift water rescue requires dry suit, PFD, and trained personnel.
▶ Watch: Underwater Lift Bag Operation
BED-04
Orange Square Bag — Blanket
AKA: Patient blanket, emergency blanket, rescue blanket
+
📖What it is

An emergency thermal blanket in an orange square bag — for patient warming during rescue and medical operations, and for protecting patients from debris and environmental exposure during extrication.

❓Why it's needed

Hypothermia is a life-threatening complication in trauma, cardiac, and drowning patients. A cold patient loses physiological stability rapidly. Warm both under AND over the patient — not just on top.

BED-05
Black Bag — Flood Light + Stand
AKA: Scene lighting, portable flood, work light
+
🔧Contents
  • Flood Light — high-output portable scene light
  • Flood Light Stand (yellow) — telescoping or folding stand to position light at optimal height
  • DeWalt Battery — cordless power for the flood light
🔧How to set up
  1. Extend/unfold the stand to the desired height.
  2. Mount the flood head to the stand — click or thread secure.
  3. Insert DeWalt battery into light.
  4. Position at scene perimeter — behind the apparatus whenever possible to avoid lighting up the road and blinding approaching drivers.
  5. Aim to light the work area, not traffic.
⚠️
Light the Work Zone — Not the RoadA flood light aimed toward approaching traffic creates a wall of glare that blinds drivers rather than helping them see the hazard. Position lights to illuminate your crew's work area with the light source pointed away from traffic.
BED-06
Orange/Red Bag — PFD + Throw Bag
AKA: Water rescue bag, throw bag bag, life ring bag
+
🔧Contents
  • 1 PFD (Personal Flotation Device) — USCG-approved life jacket for rescuer or victim
  • Throw Bag — 50–75 ft of floating rope inside a throwable bag for reach rescue without entering water
🔧Throw Bag — How to Use
  1. Open bag top — have some rope out and in your throwing hand.
  2. Throw to the victim (aim slightly past and upstream).
  3. When victim grabs the rope, hold your end firmly and pendulum them to shore — don't pull them directly toward you, let the current swing them in.
  4. Repack: stuff rope loosely back into bag — do NOT coil it — so it pays out freely on the next throw.
  5. You can throw again in seconds from a repacked bag. A coiled rope tangles.
⚠️
Reach → Throw → Row → GoThe four steps of water rescue in order. Try reach with a pole first, then throw, then row, then go in the water as a last resort with proper PPE and a safety line. Untrained in-water rescues create two victims.
▶ Watch: Throw Bag Technique
BED-07
Rope Spool — 200 ft
AKA: Utility rope, safety rope, polypropylene line
+
📖What it is

200 feet of utility rope on a spool — used for water rescue operations, perimeter control, scene management, equipment tethering, and general utility tasks.

❓Why it's needed

Rope is one of the most versatile tools in the fire service. 200 feet provides significant operational reach for water rescue safety lines, perimeter marking, and hauling operations.

✅
Know What Your Rope Is Rated ForUtility rope is not life-safety rope. Do not use it for technical rescue, rappelling, or SCBA bailout systems. Know the difference between utility rope and life-safety rope before you put weight on it.
BED-08
ABC Fire Extinguisher
AKA: Fire extinguisher, dry chem, multi-purpose extinguisher
+
📖What it is

A portable ABC dry chemical extinguisher for Class A (ordinary combustibles), Class B (flammable liquids), and Class C (electrical) fires.

🔧How to use (PASS)
  • Pull the pin
  • Aim at the base of the fire (not the flames)
  • Squeeze the handle
  • Sweep side to side
💡
Vehicle Fires Start SmallThe most effective use of this extinguisher is on small vehicle engine compartment fires caught early. Open the hood slightly, insert nozzle, sweep at the base of flames. Once the fire is established and the extinguisher can't handle it — pull back, establish a perimeter, and protect exposures.
BED-09
Sked — Foldable Stretcher
AKA: Sked, sked stretcher, sked-evac, flexible litter, drag sled
+
📖What it is

A SKED-EVAC foldable plastic stretcher that rolls up for storage and unfolds into a rigid-enough surface to drag or carry a patient across rough terrain, through narrow corridors, and on staircases. The reinforced plastic slides over most surfaces.

🔧How to use
  1. Unroll and lay flat.
  2. Position patient on the Sked.
  3. Secure straps across chest, waist, and legs.
  4. Use the drag handles at the head end for a straight-line drag.
  5. Attach rope through the head grommets for hauling up stairs or over obstacles.
  6. Two-person carry handles on the sides for lifting over very short distances.
❓Why it's needed

Standard backboards and wheeled stretchers don't work in every environment. The Sked moves patients through spaces no other device handles — collapsed structures, steep hillsides, confined spaces, and long drags over rough terrain.

▶ Watch: Sked Stretcher Patient Packaging
🪓

Truck Bed — Tools

Pike poles · Halligan · Axes · Umbrella · Snow scraper
TOOL-01
Pike Poles (×2)
AKA: Pike pole, ceiling hook, plaster hook, overhaul hook
+
📖What it is

Two pike poles — aluminum handles with a hook-and-spike tip. Used for overhaul, pulling ceilings and walls, moving debris, and water rescue reach assists.

🔧How to use
  1. For overhaul: pull wall and ceiling material toward you and to the side — NEVER directly overhead.
  2. For water rescue: extend toward a victim for reach rescue — approach from the bank, lie down to lower your center of gravity.
  3. Never stand under material you're pulling with a pike pole.
✅
Pull Toward You — Never Over YouWet, fire-damaged ceiling material is extremely heavy. Work from a protected position and pull toward you. The weight drops fast when the material lets go.
TOOL-02
Halligan Bar
AKA: Hooligan, Pro-bar, the bar, Halligan tool
+
📖What it is

A 30" forged steel multi-function forcible entry tool with a curved adze/fork at one end and a pick + flat adze at the other. The most versatile forcible entry tool in the fire service.

🔧How to use
  1. Inward-swinging door: adze end into gap at lock, drive with flat axe, rotate to lever frame and push door.
  2. Outward-swinging door: fork end behind door stop.
  3. Padlocks: hook curved end around shackle, lever.
  4. Overhead: use the pick end to punch through surfaces for pull-through.
⚠️
Try Before You PryTry the door handle first — more doors are unlocked than you expect. Forcing an unlocked door wastes time and creates unnecessary property damage.
TOOL-03
Flat Head Axe
AKA: Flat axe, striking axe, fire axe
+
📖What it is

A fire axe with a flat striking face on one side and a cutting blade on the other. Primary function with Utility 61: driving the Halligan bar and cutting through materials.

❓Why it's needed

The Halligan and flat axe together are "the irons" — the most effective forcible entry combination in the fire service. The flat face drives the Halligan with precision force.

TOOL-04
Umbrella
AKA: Personal umbrella, crew umbrella, rain cover
+
📖What it is

A standard umbrella stored with the tool complement for crew comfort during extended outdoor operations in rain — protecting documentation, patient care activities, and equipment from precipitation.

❓Why it's needed

Utility 61 handles extended support operations. Keeping paper documentation, electronic equipment, and patients dry during outdoor incidents in rain is a genuine operational need — not a comfort item.

TOOL-05
Snow Scraper
AKA: Ice scraper, windshield scraper
+
📖What it is

A standard automotive snow and ice scraper for clearing the windshield and windows before operation in winter conditions.

❓Why it's needed

Driving a utility vehicle with an obstructed windshield is a crash risk — and a legal liability. Clear snow and ice before moving, not after you're rolling.

⚠️
Clear ALL Windows — Not Just Driver's ViewClear front, back, and side windows completely. A snow-covered rear window means no rear visibility. A snow-covered hood means sliding snow can obstruct forward view while driving.
🔋

Supplies — Batteries & Hydration

Spare DeWalt batteries · Water bottles
SUP-01
Spare DeWalt Batteries
AKA: Spare batteries, tool batteries, 20V batteries, cordless batteries
+
📖What it is

Spare DeWalt 20V MAX or FLEXVOLT battery packs compatible with the flood light and any other DeWalt cordless tools stored in the bed.

❓Why it's needed

Cordless tools are only as good as their battery. A flood light that dies midway through a technical rescue operation is a serious problem. Spare batteries eliminate that single point of failure.

✅
Check Charge Level Every ShiftBatteries self-discharge sitting on the apparatus. A battery that was full on Monday may be at 30% by Friday. Check every shift — fully charge any battery below 50%.
SUP-02
Water Bottles
AKA: Crew hydration, water supply
+
📖What it is

Water for crew hydration stored in the truck bed — accessible during and after operations.

❓Why it's needed

Firefighting, technical rescue, and extended scene operations cause significant fluid loss through exertion and heat. Dehydration impairs cognitive function and physical performance before you feel thirsty. Drink proactively.

💡
Hydrate Before — Not Just AfterDrink before the shift, before the call if possible, and immediately after coming off a working assignment. Waiting until you feel thirsty means you're already dehydrated.
✅

Probationary Firefighter Field Reference

Brushtruck 62

Compartment-by-Compartment Study Guide
Before you start: You don't memorize the truck — you understand it. When you know why every piece of gear is there and what problem it solves, the whole truck makes sense as a system. Walk up to the rig and physically touch the items as you study. Tactile memory is just as important as book memory.
01 · Front Seat 02 · Glove Box 03 · Back Seat 04 · Container 05 · Rear Water 06 · Hand Tools 07 · Water Pump 08 · Hydrant Bag
01
Section 1
Front Seat
1 item
📻
Radios
Portable / HT / Handie-Talkie
▶
Battery-powered handheld transceivers that allow voice communication between crew members, command, dispatch, and mutual aid agencies. Programmed with your agency's tactical channels, mutual aid frequencies, and standard ICS channels. At least one radio per seat position is standard on a brush truck.
  1. Power on and confirm full battery charge — this is part of your daily rig check, non-negotiable.
  2. Confirm you're on the correct assigned channel before leaving the station.
  3. To transmit: press and hold PTT, wait one full second before speaking to prevent clipping your first word.
  4. Speak clearly at a normal pace, directly into the mic. Release PTT when finished.
  5. Use ICS radio discipline — identify yourself, then your message: "Command from Engine 62 — water supply established."
  6. Monitor your assigned channel. Never switch channels without notifying your officer.
⚡
Rookie Alert — Radio Discipline
Never key your radio while someone else is transmitting — this "steps on" their message and can block a critical communication. Wait for the channel to clear. Also: always verify your channel before operating. A firefighter who can't reach command is a firefighter in danger.
The radio is your primary tool for situational awareness, hazard reporting, resource requests, and crew accountability. On a brush fire, conditions change in seconds — a wind shift, a flare-up, a spot fire across a road. Without communication, you are isolated. With it, you are part of a team.
Also Known AsPortable, handie-talkie, HT, brick, walkie-talkie, portable radio
02
Section 2
Glove Box
4 items
📗
ERG Book
Emergency Response Guidebook
▶
The Emergency Response Guidebook — published by the U.S. DOT — is a pocket-sized reference used to identify hazardous materials and determine initial safe response actions. It's organized by UN/NA placard numbers, chemical names, and color-coded guide pages for isolation distances. A new edition is published every four years — always ensure your copy is current.
  1. Identify the 4-digit UN/NA number on the vehicle's placard.
  2. Look it up in the yellow (numerical) or blue (alphabetical) index pages.
  3. Note the guide number referenced (e.g., Guide 128).
  4. Turn to the orange-bordered guide page for that number.
  5. Read Potential Hazards first — fire/explosion risk and health hazards.
  6. Follow the Public Safety section for initial isolation distances.
  7. For large spills or fires, use the green-bordered Table of Initial Isolation and Protective Action Distances.
  8. Relay findings to your officer and dispatch immediately.
Watch: How to Use the ERG
Brush fires don't stay in the wildland — they reach propane tanks, agricultural chemical storage, and vehicles with hazmat placards. Before you get close to anything with a placard, you need to know what you're dealing with. The ERG is your first line of reference when electronic resources aren't available.
Also Known AsEmergency Response Guidebook, DOT guide, hazmat book, orange book
🪲
Bug Spray
Insect Repellent / DEET
▶
A commercial DEET-based insect repellent stored in the glove box for use during extended brush fire operations and mop-up in vegetation-heavy areas.
  1. Apply to exposed skin and clothing before entering tall grass, underbrush, or wooded areas.
  2. Spray into your hands first before applying near the face — never spray directly at your face.
  3. Do not apply inside enclosed vehicles or spaces.
  4. Reapply per manufacturer guidance during extended operations.
Wildland firefighting involves extended time in environments where ticks and mosquitoes are active. Tick-borne illnesses like Lyme disease are a genuine occupational hazard for first responders working in the field. This is not an afterthought item.
Also Known AsInsect repellent, DEET spray, tick spray
🔑
Fuel Key
Fleet Card / Pump Key
▶
A specialized fleet key or card that grants access to the department's fueling station (Glen Ellyn fuel station) for refueling Brushtruck 62's main vehicle tank.
  1. Drive to the designated fuel station.
  2. Insert or swipe the key/card to authorize the pump.
  3. Fuel the correct tank — know your fuel type before you pull up to the pump.
  4. Log the transaction per department policy.
  5. Return the key to the glove box immediately after use.
⚡
Rookie Alert — Fuel Type
Know your fuel type before touching the nozzle. The truck's main engine likely takes diesel. The portable pump takes gasoline. Putting gasoline in a diesel engine causes catastrophic damage. When in doubt, ask your officer first.
Fleet fuel cards prevent unauthorized use, enable accurate fuel tracking, and grant access to secured pumps. Losing this key is an administrative and operational problem — treat it like your own car keys.
Also Known AsFleet card, fuel card, pump key
🗺️
Water Guides / Water Source Maps
Rural Water Supply Maps
▶
Printed reference maps identifying pre-surveyed natural water sources in your response area — ponds, streams, swimming pools, cisterns, dry hydrants, and other potential drafting locations. May be laminated map sheets or a bound booklet.
  1. When the tank is running low and no hydrant is available, pull the guide.
  2. Identify your current location and reference the nearest marked water source.
  3. Relay the location to your officer for routing.
  4. Note any access limitations — weight-restricted bridges, narrow lanes, or locked gates that could trap apparatus.
Hydrants don't exist in wildland and rural areas. Knowing where you can draft water is a critical tactical advantage — it's what extends your truck's capability beyond the 250 gallons onboard. These guides represent pre-work your predecessors did so you don't have to figure it out under pressure.
Also Known AsWater source maps, drafting location guide, pre-survey maps, rural water supply maps
03
Section 3
Back Seat
4 items
🦺
PFD — Personal Flotation Device
Life Jacket / Life Vest
▶
A Type III or Type V Coast Guard-approved life jacket — foam or inflatable — worn around the torso to maintain buoyancy in water. Keeps a person afloat even if incapacitated.
  1. Pull the PFD over your head and secure all buckles and straps snugly.
  2. Fit check: it should not ride up over your chin when you pull upward on the front hem.
  3. For inflatable models: confirm the CO₂ cartridge is installed and the armed indicator is green before operating near water.
  4. Wear any time you are within arm's reach of an open water source during drafting, vehicle operations near water, or other water-hazard scenarios.
  5. Inspect before use: check for tears, missing buckles, and buoyancy integrity.
⚡
Critical Safety — "I'm Not Going in the Water"
The most dangerous words near any water hazard. The PFD goes on before the incident, not after you fall in. Drowning is a documented firefighter line-of-duty fatality category. If your crew is working near a pond, creek, or any open water — PFD goes on. No discussion needed.
Brush fires frequently occur near retention ponds, drainage ditches, rivers, and flooded areas. Firefighters hauling hard suction hose to a drafting point are often working at the water's edge on slippery terrain while fatigued and carrying equipment. A slip can happen in seconds.
Also Known AsLife jacket, life vest, flotation device, PFD
Watch: Fitting and Inspecting a PFD
⚡
Hot Stick
Voltage Detector / Electrical Safety Rod
▶
An insulated fiberglass pole (4–6 feet) used to safely probe areas near potential electrical hazards without direct contact. Some versions include an audible/visual voltage detection indicator. Allows firefighters to test whether vegetation, fencing, or debris near a power line is energized before touching it.
  1. Extend the hot stick to its full working length.
  2. Approach the suspected hazard from the side — keep your body as far from the hazard as the stick allows.
  3. If voltage-detecting model: hold near (not touching) the suspected conductor and watch/listen for the indicator.
  4. If probing only: use the tip to touch debris near lines — never grab or pull potentially energized material.
  5. Never use a wet hot stick — moisture compromises electrical insulation.
  6. If voltage is detected or you're unsure: back off, establish a hazard perimeter, notify your IC, and contact the utility company.
⚡
Critical Safety — Step Potential
Assume every downed power line is live. Current can energize the ground around a downed line — a phenomenon called "step potential." Stay a minimum of one full span (pole-to-pole distance) away. The hot stick reduces risk; it does not eliminate it.
Brush fires regularly down power lines and energize surrounding areas — fences, trees, soil, and standing water can all carry current. You cannot tell if something is energized by looking at it. The hot stick creates a safe buffer between you and potential electrocution.
Also Known AsVoltage detector, proximity tester, electrical safety rod, lineman's stick
Watch: Hot Stick and Electrical Safety
🔦
Box Light (Large Flashlight)
Scene Light / Hand Lantern
▶
A high-powered, rechargeable handheld flashlight — lantern or box-style — with significantly higher lumen output than a personal flashlight. Designed to illuminate large areas during nighttime or reduced-visibility operations.
  1. Confirm full battery charge at the start of every shift.
  2. At night or in smoke-reduced visibility, deploy to illuminate work areas, staging zones, or access routes.
  3. Can be set down as a scene light while you work hands-free.
  4. Return to back seat and place on charger (if docking-style) at end of shift.
Brush fires don't stop at sunset, and wildland environments have zero ambient light. Mop-up operations, overhaul, and crew accountability all require reliable illumination. The box light supplements personal headlamps with broader scene coverage.
Also Known AsScene light, hand lantern, big flashlight, spot lantern, flood light
🎒
Hose Bag
Forestry Hose Bag / Deployment Bag
▶
A canvas or nylon bag pre-loaded with folded 1-inch forestry hose for rapid deployment. Allows one firefighter to carry a significant hose load without tangling or premature unrolling.
  1. Shoulder or carry the bag to your deployment position.
  2. Connect the male end to your water source (pump outlet, inline valve, or wye).
  3. Walk toward the fire edge while a partner holds the source connection.
  4. Open the bag and allow hose to feed out as you advance.
  5. Attach your nozzle to the female end once fully deployed.
Pre-packed hose bags allow rapid, tangle-free deployment through brush terrain where dragging a rolled hose through vegetation would be slow and inefficient. Speed matters in initial brush fire attack — the faster water goes on fire, the smaller the fire stays.
Also Known AsForestry hose bag, pre-connected line, deployment bag, wildland hose bag
04
Section 4
Container in Back Seat
9 items
🌀
Small 1″ Hose
Forestry Line / Wildland Hose
▶
A section of 1-inch diameter single-jacket forestry hose — lighter and more flexible than structural attack hose. Standard NST threaded couplings. This is a backup section stored in the container, separate from the reel.
Connect to the pump's 1-inch discharge or an inline valve. Use for spot extinguishment, mop-up, or as an extension when the main hose reel line can't reach. Can also be handed off to a second crew working a separate flank.
Fires don't cooperate with fixed hose lengths. A backup section means extra reach, a secondary line, or flexibility to hand off to another crew without giving up your primary line.
Also Known AsForestry line, one-inch line, wildland hose, booster hose
🟡
Safety Vest
Hi-Vis Vest / Reflective Vest
▶
A Class II or III ANSI-compliant high-visibility vest — bright orange or lime green with retro-reflective striping — worn over PPE to make firefighters visible to vehicle traffic. Non-structural; visual protection only.
  1. Pull over your head and secure any side straps or zipper.
  2. Wear any time you are operating within or adjacent to active traffic lanes, on a roadway shoulder, or where vehicle traffic is present.
  3. At night, retro-reflective strips become even more critical — don't skip it after dark.
⚡
Rookie Alert — "We'll Only Be a Minute"
There is no operation short enough to skip the vest near traffic. Fatal line-of-duty deaths have occurred in under 60 seconds of roadside exposure. It takes 5 seconds to put on. There is no excuse.
Firefighters are struck and killed by vehicles at emergency scenes every year. Drivers in emergencies do not slow down adequately, and dark turnout gear blends into night. The vest makes you visible from hundreds of feet away.
Also Known AsHi-vis vest, traffic vest, reflective vest, ANSI vest, safety vest
🗺️
Maps
Street Map / Response District Map
▶
Printed street, aerial, or tactical maps of your response district — possibly laminated. May include hydrant maps, response boundaries, and mutual aid overlaps.
When GPS fails, the map is your navigation backup. Also use to brief incoming mutual aid crews on access routes, establish staging areas, and communicate geographic reference points to units that don't know your district.
GPS dead zones exist. Cell towers go down. Batteries die. Paper maps never lose signal. On a large incident with multiple access routes and incoming mutual aid, a physical map is the fastest way to communicate geography to everyone simultaneously.
Also Known AsStreet map, Thomas Guide, district map, response map, area map
🟫
Duct Tape
100-MPH Tape / Rigger's Tape
▶
Heavy-duty cloth-backed pressure-sensitive adhesive tape — one of the most versatile field tools in any kit.
Temporary repair of leaking hose, securing loose equipment, marking hazards, labeling gear, temporarily repairing torn PPE, sealing openings, and hundreds of other field applications. On long extended-attack operations, field improvisation is a survival skill.
Equipment fails in the field. Duct tape buys time. A leaking hose coupling that can't be immediately swapped can be temporarily wrapped to reduce flow loss. The moment you need it and don't have it, you'll never skip packing it again.
Also Known AsDuck tape, 100-mph tape, rigger's tape, gaffer tape
⚠️
Caution Tape
Barrier Tape / Scene Tape
▶
Brightly colored (yellow/black) polyethylene barrier tape printed with "CAUTION" or "DO NOT ENTER." Visual warning only — not a physical barrier.
  1. Attach one end to a fixed anchor point (tree, post, door handle).
  2. Walk the perimeter of the hazard zone, unspooling as you go.
  3. Tie off at regular intervals to maintain taut lines.
  4. Keep at a visible height — roughly waist-to-chest level.
Establishes visual hazard perimeters for unprotected bystanders, marks unstable ground, defines fire lines, identifies electrical hazard zones, and restricts civilian access — without requiring a firefighter to stand there indefinitely.
Also Known AsBarrier tape, police tape, scene tape, hazard tape
🗑️
Garbage Bags
Contractor Bags / Heavy-Duty Bags
▶
Heavy-duty plastic bags — typically contractor-grade, 3-mil or heavier — carried in quantity for field use.
Collect fire debris and contaminated materials during overhaul. Bag compromised PPE. Improvise waterproofing for electronics or documents. Contain sharps or biological hazard materials. Manage scene waste during extended operations.
Overhaul generates waste. Proper disposal of contaminated materials is both an environmental requirement and a secondary exposure safeguard. On a multi-hour operation, organized waste management keeps the work area safe.
Also Known AsTrash bags, contractor bags, heavy-duty bags, debris bags
📚
Pub Ed — Public Education Materials
Fire Prevention / Community Outreach
▶
Pre-printed educational materials — stickers, magnets, or card stock — intended for distribution during non-emergency community contacts. May include fire prevention tips, emergency numbers, smoke alarm reminders, and department contact information.
Distribute to homeowners, bystanders, or members of the public during non-emergency contacts, public events, or fire prevention moments that arise naturally during and after incidents.
Fire prevention is the best fire protection. Every sticker handed to a homeowner is a potential reminder to test their smoke alarm, clear brush, or call before burning. Community trust and prevention are core parts of the job.
Also Known AsFire prevention materials, PubEd, community education, public outreach, prevention stickers
🪢
Strap (Utility / Tie-Down)
Tie-Down / Ratchet Strap
▶
A nylon or polyester webbing strap — typically 1–2 inches wide — with a ratchet mechanism or cam buckle for securing loads during transport or field use.
Use to secure equipment during transport, lash hose to brush for anchoring, secure debris during overhaul, or improvise a drag handle. Release ratchet straps by pulling the release lever; rewind neatly for next use.
Equipment that shifts in a moving truck is a safety hazard. Straps keep your load organized and your compartment ready for the next call.
Also Known AsTie-down strap, ratchet strap, cam strap, lashing, webbing strap
🧻
Towel
Utility Towel / Shop Rag
▶
A heavy-duty utility cloth or shop-style towel for operational use. Not for personal hygiene — this is a work towel.
Wipe down tools after use, clean pump connections, dry hose fittings before coupling, or use as an improvisational pad or wrap.
Dirt and debris on hose threads prevent solid coupling and damage gaskets. Keeping couplings clean and dry ensures watertight connections under pressure. Small thing, big consequences when it fails mid-operation.
Also Known AsUtility towel, shop rag, work towel
05
Section 5
Rear of Vehicle — Water System
10 items
💧
250-Gallon Water Tank
Booster Tank / Onboard Water
▶
A truck-mounted poly or fiberglass tank holding 250 gallons — the onboard supply that makes Brushtruck 62 a mobile attack unit. At 25–30 GPM through a 1-inch line, 250 gallons gives you roughly 8–10 minutes of continuous water. Plan accordingly.
The tank feeds the onboard pump. Check and confirm full at the start of every shift. Fill via the tank fill inlet on the pump panel or rear access. Monitor your level during operations — communicate it to your officer at 50% and again at 25%.
⚡
Rookie Alert — Never Surprise Your Officer
Never let the tank run dry without warning. Call it out: "IC, we're at half tank" at 125 gallons. "IC, quarter tank" at ~60 gallons. A dry truck with a crew in the field is a life-safety event. When the pump cavitates (runs without water), impeller damage follows fast.
Provides immediate water supply without needing a hydrant — this is what makes initial brush fire attack possible in areas with zero water infrastructure. It's your autonomy as a mobile unit.
Also Known AsBooster tank, onboard water, water tank, tank water, portable tank
🎡
1″ Hose Reel (200 Feet)
Booster Reel / Wildland Attack Line
▶
A motorized or manual reel mounted to the truck storing 200 feet of 1-inch booster/forestry hose in a continuous coil. Always connected to the pump — allows extension and retraction without removing from the truck. The truck can drive with the hose deployed.
  1. Open the reel discharge valve on the pump panel.
  2. Pull the nozzle end from the reel and walk toward the fire.
  3. Hose unspools from the reel as you advance.
  4. When finished: close nozzle, bleed residual pressure, then rewind the reel (motorized: use reel motor switch; manual: use the crank handle).
  5. Lay hose flat and even on the reel — crossed or bunched hose jams the reel.
Watch: Hose Reel Deployment
Your primary initial attack tool. Fast, always connected, and allows progressive hose lays — extending hose as the truck repositions without disconnecting anything. Truck to water on fire in under 60 seconds.
Also Known AsBooster reel, reel line, 1-inch reel, wildland attack line, hose reel
🔧
Handle for Hose Reel
Reel Crank / Manual Winding Handle
▶
A detachable crank handle used to manually rewind the hose reel when the motorized drive is unavailable or has failed.
Insert into the reel's drive socket and crank in the winding direction (typically clockwise facing the reel). Maintain even tension on the hose as you crank to prevent bunching. Store in its designated bracket when not in use.
If the motorized reel motor fails, you still need to recover 200 feet of hose without leaving it on the ground. The manual handle is your backup — don't leave it behind at the station.
Also Known AsReel crank, winding handle, manual reel handle
🪣
Hard Suction Hose (2 × 12′ Black)
Hard Suction / Drafting Hose
▶
Rigid, wire-reinforced PVC hose that does NOT collapse under negative pressure — unlike standard attack hose. Allows the pump to draw from a static source below pump level. Each of 2 sections is 12 feet; combined reach is 24 feet. Black and noticeably stiffer than fire hose.
  1. Connect the two sections together — hand tight plus a quarter-turn with a spanner.
  2. Attach the metal strainer to the source end (the end going into the water).
  3. Thread the pump end into the pump's suction intake (2½-inch or larger inlet).
  4. Lower the strainer end into the water — fully submerged, ideally 2+ feet under the surface to prevent vortexing.
  5. Prime the pump and begin drafting.
  6. After use: flush both sections, inspect for cracks, and store in their designated brackets.
⚡
Critical Safety — Air Leaks Kill Drafting Operations
Every connection must be airtight. A single loose coupling introduces air into the suction line, destroys your prime, and you have no water. Feel and listen for air leaks at every joint. Never run the pump at high RPM without water in the suction line — pump damage occurs fast when running dry.
Watch: Drafting with Hard Suction Hose
With this equipment, your truck can draw from any nearby pond, creek, or swimming pool — essentially unlimited water supply. Without it, you are limited to 250 gallons. It's the difference between sustained attack and retreat.
Also Known AsHard suction, suction hose, drafting hose, rigid suction, hard sleeve
🕸️
Metal Filter / Strainer for Suction Hose
Suction Strainer / Basket Strainer / Draft Strainer
▶
A dome-shaped or cylindrical metal screen that attaches to the source (water) end of the hard suction hose and sits inside the water source during drafting operations.
Thread or snap onto the end of the hard suction hose before inserting into the water. Submerge at least 2 feet below the surface. After use: remove, rinse clean, and inspect for dents or torn screen material.
Natural water sources contain leaves, sticks, sediment, algae, and aquatic life. Without the strainer, any of this material can enter the pump, clog impellers, damage seals, and destroy a pump worth thousands of dollars. The strainer is cheap insurance — don't draft without it.
Also Known AsSuction strainer, foot valve, draft strainer, basket strainer, pump strainer
🧱
Metal Wheel Chock (1)
Chock Block / Wheel Block
▶
A wedge-shaped block placed under a tire to prevent vehicle movement when parked on a grade or during pump operations.
Place firmly against the downhill side of a rear tire before engaging the pump or leaving the vehicle unattended on any slope. Position diagonally so the vehicle can't roll forward or backward.
⚠️
Rookie Alert — Build the Habit Now
Chocking the wheel before leaving the cab is a habit you build now. At a brush fire on a hillside, a rolling apparatus could kill someone. Drop the chock first, every time, before anything else — even before the radio. OSHA requires it. More importantly, lives depend on it.
During pump operations, the engine is running and the drivetrain is engaged. If the truck starts rolling on a slope, it can injure crew members working near hose connections or run into the fire itself. Two seconds to drop the chock can save a life.
Also Known AsChock block, wheel block, parking wedge, tire chock
⛽
Plastic Gas Can (Pump Fuel)
Jerry Can / Portable Fuel Container
▶
A red or yellow portable gas can containing unleaded gasoline — fuel for the portable water pump's gasoline engine. This is NOT for the truck's main engine (which is likely diesel).
  1. Shut down and allow the portable pump to cool slightly before refueling.
  2. Use the plastic funnel (stored with tools) to avoid spills.
  3. Fill to the marked fill line — never overfill.
  4. Replace the cap securely before restarting.
  5. Store upright in its bracket, away from ignition sources.
  6. Check fuel level during every rig check.
⚡
Critical Safety — No Open Flames During Fueling
Refuel only with the pump off and cooled for at least 2 minutes. Gasoline vapors ignite from exhaust components, hot engine surfaces, and static electricity. No smoking. Keep ignition sources away. Always use the funnel — spilling fuel near a hot engine is how fires start at the truck.
The portable pump is only useful if it has fuel. Running out of gas during an active drafting operation is a completely preventable failure. Check it every shift. Carry extra.
Also Known AsGas can, jerry can, fuel can, portable fuel container
🌀
2½″ Hose Roll (50 Feet)
Two-and-a-Half / Supply Hose
▶
A 50-foot roll of 2½-inch diameter woven-jacket fire hose — larger-diameter supply and relay hose. Significantly heavier and stiffer than forestry hose. Can flow 250+ GPM depending on pressure.
Deploy as a supply line from a hydrant to your pump, or as a relay line between two apparatus. Connect male end to the water source, female end to your pump intake. Tighten couplings with the large spanner.
When you need to move large volumes of water — supplying your brush truck from a hydrant, establishing a relay, or connecting to an engine company — the 2½-inch line moves it. The 1-inch line doesn't have the volume for these applications.
Also Known AsTwo-and-a-half inch, two-and-a-half line, big line, relay hose, supply hose, 2½
🌀
1½″ Hose on Cross Lay (~150 Feet)
Inch-and-a-Half / Cross-Lay Attack Line
▶
Approximately 150 feet of 1½-inch diameter attack hose pre-loaded on a cross-lay bed — a compartment allowing deployment from either side of the truck. Heavier and more durable than 1-inch forestry hose; designed for medium-duty attack applications and flowing roughly 95–125 GPM.
  1. Pull from the side of the cross-lay closest to your attack point.
  2. Walk the load toward the fire while a partner makes the pump connection.
  3. Advance the line and open the nozzle at the attack point.
  4. After use: wash, drain, and reload flat on the cross-lay bed.
Bridges the gap between the 1-inch reel (fast and light, limited flow) and the 2½-inch supply line (high volume, awkward to advance). The 1½-inch gives enough flow for a structural exposure or heavier brush fire while remaining manageable for 1–2 firefighters.
Also Known AsOne-and-a-half inch, inch-and-a-half, attack line, cross-lay line, 1½
💦
Fog Nozzle
Combination Nozzle / Adjustable Fog Nozzle
▶
A variable-pattern nozzle adjustable from straight (solid) stream to wide fog — multiple settings in between. Fog pattern breaks water into fine droplets, dramatically increasing surface area and cooling capacity. Design pressure typically 100 PSI; flow 30–250 GPM depending on size and setting.
  1. Straight stream: maximum reach and penetration. Use for heavy fuels or reaching flame from distance.
  2. Narrow fog (30°): combination of reach and cooling. Good general attack pattern.
  3. Wide fog (60–90°): maximum cooling and heat shielding. Use for exposure protection, vapor suppression, or defensive withdrawal.
  4. To shut off: rotate the bail or handle to closed position. Never leave a charged hose unattended with an open nozzle.
⚠️
Rookie Alert — Fog Patterns in Wind
Wide fog in high-wind conditions will deflect your water and can push heat back at you. In windy brush fire conditions, use a tighter pattern or straight stream for better control over where your water actually goes. Read the wind before you set your pattern.
Watch: Fog Nozzle Patterns and Techniques
Fire behavior in brush is unpredictable. The fog nozzle gives you tactical flexibility in a single tool — attack flame, cool exposures, and protect yourself without swapping tips. The wide fog pattern also cools embers in the air and reduces re-ignition during mop-up.
Also Known AsCombination nozzle, adjustable fog nozzle, fog tip, TFT nozzle, Akron nozzle
06
Section 6
Rear of Vehicle — Hand Tools
6 items
🪶
Brush Paddles (3 Total)
Fire Swatter / Flapper / Beater
▶
A flat rubber or woven-fiber paddle on a long wooden handle — used to beat out flames in light fuels. Looks unsophisticated; works exceptionally well in the right conditions. Three are carried to allow crew teamwork.
  1. Approach from the side — never from downwind or directly ahead of the flame front.
  2. Strike with a firm, flat-angle downward slap, dragging the paddle slightly toward you — this smothers the fire by cutting oxygen and pushing burning fuel together.
  3. Work in short strokes, moving parallel to the fire edge (not perpendicular into it).
  4. Rest the paddle periodically — rubber paddles melt or tear with continuous flame contact.
  5. Two firefighters working in tandem (leap-frog smothering) suppress a line faster than one working alone.
⚡
Critical Safety — Wind and Fire Behavior
Never position yourself ahead of or downwind of the flame front. Fire spreads fastest with the wind. If it jumps over you, you are trapped. Always work from the black (burned area) or from the flanks. Always maintain an escape route.
Watch: Brush Paddle Technique
In light, fine fuels — grass, hay, weeds — water is often unnecessary and slower than direct suppression. A paddle knocks down a grass fire edge faster than deploying a hose. No water supply needed, no setup time — pick it up and go.
Also Known AsFire swatter, flapper, beater, brush flap, wildland paddle, fire flap
🪝
Pike Poles (2 Total)
Pike / Hook / Overhaul Hook
▶
A long wooden or fiberglass pole with a sharp metal hook at the end — the hook has a pointed tip and a curved "pike" protruding from the side. One of the oldest tools in the fire service. Typically 6, 8, or 10 feet long.
  1. Use the point to probe, push, or pull burning or smoldering material.
  2. Use the hook to pull burning debris apart, exposing hot spots to air and water.
  3. During overhaul: hook and pull burning logs, stumps, or brush piles to separate fuel and expose embers.
  4. Never use near energized electrical equipment — wooden handles offer some insulation but are NOT rated for electrical work.
  5. Work at arm's length — the tool exists to keep your body away from the heat.
Watch: Pike Pole Use and Overhaul
Overhaul after a brush fire requires breaking apart heavy fuels — root masses, logs, thick brush — to ensure no smoldering spots can reignite. You cannot do this safely with your hands. The pike pole keeps you out of direct heat.
Also Known AsPike, hook, rubbish hook, ceiling hook (structural), overhaul hook
🪝
New York Pole / Roof Rake (1)
NY Hook / New York Hook / Heavy Hook
▶
A heavy-duty version of the pike pole — typically 10–12 feet with a more substantial, wider hook profile. Originally designed for pulling apart roof sections in structural firefighting; equally useful in the wildland-urban interface for moving large debris, pulling fence rails, or dislodging heavy burning material.
Same technique as the standard pike pole but designed for heavier material and greater reach. The wider hook catches larger debris. Use where the standard pike pole isn't heavy or long enough for the job — heavy root balls, fence lines, structural debris.
When the standard pike pole isn't enough, the New York pole steps up. Greater leverage, greater mechanical advantage, greater reach on heavy material. At the wildland-urban interface, you encounter structures — and this tool handles the heavy end of debris work.
Also Known AsNew York hook, NY hook, roofing hook, heavy hook, roof rake
✂️
Bolt Cutters
Fence Cutters / Chain Cutters
▶
Heavy-duty compound-action cutting tool with hardened steel jaws, designed to cut padlocks, chain link, wire, fence cable, and small rebar. Typically 24–36 inches long with cushion-grip handles.
  1. Open the jaws fully.
  2. Position material to be cut as deep in the jaw as possible — cutting near the pivot provides maximum mechanical advantage.
  3. Apply firm, even pressure on both handles simultaneously.
  4. Keep fingers and face clear of the jaw line.
  5. After use: wipe clean and store in the designated bracket.
⚠️
Rookie Alert — Document What You Cut
Cutting a lock or fence has legal implications. Always document it — notify your officer, note the location in the incident report, and if possible note the owner's contact information for department follow-up. Cut first if life safety requires it, but never forget to document.
Brush fires don't respect property lines, and rural landowners lock everything. Fence lines block access roads, locked gates prevent apparatus entry to fields and pastures, and wire on the ground creates tire hazards. Bolt cutters get you through all of it fast.
Also Known AsBolt cutters, fence cutters, wire cutters, chain cutters
⚙️
Halligan Tool ("Hallagan Tool")
Halligan Bar / The Bar / Irons
▶
A multi-purpose forcible entry tool — a steel bar (~30 inches, 8–10 lbs) with three working ends: an adze (horizontal wedge blade), a pick, and a fork (two-tine wedge). Often paired with a flathead axe — this combination is called "the irons." Note: often spelled "Hallagan" in the field — both are understood.
Fork/Adze end: Insert between a door and frame at the latch to pry the door open.

Pick end: Drive into wood or soil for purchase; break padlocks; penetrate materials.

Adze: Chop, pry, dig, breach.

In the brush context: pry open shed doors, break padlocked gates, dig fire lines, or pry apart debris at the wildland-urban interface.
⚠️
Rookie Alert — Know Your Ends Before the Incident
Every Halligan is forged — the pick and fork are specific orientations. Learn which end does what before the call. When paired with a flathead axe (the irons): the fork is married to the door gap and the axe drives it. Practice this before you need it. Fumbling at a burning building is not the time to learn.
Watch: Halligan Bar Forcible Entry
At the wildland-urban interface, locked doors become life-safety problems during evacuations or when fire threatens occupants. The Halligan is the most versatile hand tool in the fire service for rapid entry. No firefighter should be unfamiliar with it.
Also Known AsHalligan bar, hooligan tool, pry bar, the bar, irons (paired with axe), Hallagan bar
🫙
Plastic Funnel
Fuel Funnel / Pouring Funnel
▶
A standard wide-mouth plastic funnel (6–8 inches across at the top) used to direct gasoline from the gas can into the portable pump's fuel tank without spilling.
Insert the spout into the pump's fuel tank opening. Pour gasoline from the gas can through the funnel slowly to avoid overflow. Remove and wipe down after use. Store in its bracket.
Spilling gasoline near a running engine or hot exhaust components is a fire and burn injury hazard. The funnel eliminates that risk. Simple tool, important function — and the one most likely to be skipped "just this once" by someone in a hurry.
Also Known AsFuel funnel, pouring funnel
07
Section 7
Water Pump
1 item
⚙️
Portable Water Pump — 2½″ Inlet / 1½″ Outlet
Gas Pump / Honda Pump / Drafting Pump
▶
A small, gasoline-powered centrifugal pump — self-contained with its own engine (separate from the truck's engine), 2½-inch suction intake, and 1½-inch discharge outlet. Designed to draft water from natural sources when the truck's onboard pump is not optimally positioned, or to supplement supply at remote locations.
  1. Position the pump as close to water level as practical — centrifugal pumps have a lift limit (typically 10–25 feet).
  2. Connect hard suction hose with metal strainer to the 2½-inch inlet.
  3. Connect attack or supply hose to the 1½-inch outlet.
  4. Check fuel level and oil level per manufacturer markings.
  5. Cold start: choke on → pull starter cord firmly → advance choke as engine warms → set operating throttle.
  6. Prime the pump if required (primer bulb or manual priming pump on some models).
  7. Confirm water flowing at discharge before advancing throttle fully.
  8. Shutdown: reduce throttle → move choke to off/run → shut off fuel valve → allow to cool before moving.
⚡
Critical Safety — Inlet/Outlet Are Not Interchangeable
The 2½-inch is the inlet (suction side). The 1½-inch is the outlet (discharge side). Flow goes one direction through a centrifugal pump. Connecting to the wrong port gives you zero water. Also: never run the pump dry — if prime is lost, shut down immediately and re-prime before restarting. Impeller damage occurs rapidly without water.
Watch: Portable Fire Pump Operations
Gives you a remote water supply capability — position the pump at a pond or creek while the truck stays on the road or in a defensible position. Also serves as a backup if the truck's main pump has issues. In rural firefighting, the ability to draft from any available source is critical to sustained operations.
Also Known AsPortable pump, gas pump, Honda pump (brand-generic), trash pump, drafting pump
08
Section 8
Hydrant Bag
9 items
🚰
Gate Valve
Hydrant Gate / Auxiliary Valve / HAV
▶
A large-diameter valve installed between a hydrant outlet and your supply line, giving you local on/off flow control without shutting down the entire hydrant.
  1. Connect the gate valve directly to the hydrant outlet before opening the hydrant.
  2. Open the hydrant fully — hydrants are designed for full open or full closed; never throttle at the stem.
  3. Control flow using the gate valve's handwheel.
  4. When done: close gate valve first, then close hydrant, then bleed the line.
Without a gate valve, your only flow control is the hydrant itself — repeatedly opening and closing damages the seat. The gate valve maintains full hydrant pressure while you independently manage flow to your lines. Essential for tanker fill operations and multi-hose setups.
Also Known AsHydrant gate, gate valve, auxiliary valve, hydrant assist valve (HAV)
🪣
1″ Garden Hose
Garden Hose / Flush Hose
▶
Standard residential garden hose with standard garden-hose threaded fittings — smaller diameter, lower pressure than fire hose.
Used to flush hydrants before connecting supply lines — hydrants accumulate sediment you don't want entering your pump. Also used for light-duty applications: washing down equipment, filling water coolers, or supplying a water source for hand tool cleanup.
Hydrant flushing before connection is standard procedure that's easy to skip and costly if you don't. Sediment in a pump is expensive damage. The garden hose makes flushing quick and simple.
Also Known AsGarden hose, flush hose
🔩
Hydrant Wrench
Hydrant Key / Pentagon Wrench
▶
A specialized wrench designed to fit the pentagonal (5-sided) operating nut on a fire hydrant — the bolt on top that opens and closes the main valve.
  1. Place the wrench socket over the operating nut.
  2. Open counterclockwise in most US jurisdictions — "lefty loosey."
  3. Open fully — hydrants are designed for full-open operation.
  4. Close clockwise until fully seated.
  5. Never use excessive force — hydrant stems can break, causing uncontrolled water release.
Watch: Opening a Fire Hydrant
Most fire hydrants cannot be opened without this wrench — they're intentionally designed to resist unauthorized opening. Without it, you have zero hydrant water supply.
Also Known AsHydrant key, pentagon wrench, hydrant valve key, fire hydrant wrench
🔧
Small Spanner Wrench (1¾″ Hose / Gas Shut-Off)
Spanner / Hose Wrench / Coupling Wrench
▶
A flat, open-ended wrench with a pin or lug that engages the lugs on a hose coupling — used to tighten or loosen 1¾-inch hose connections. The slot end can also operate a gas meter shut-off valve.
Insert the pin into a lug hole on the coupling and use the wrench as a lever to rotate the coupling tight. For gas meter shut-off: insert the wrench slot over the valve and rotate 90 degrees to shut off. Always tighten in the closing direction, loosen in the opening direction — know your coupling orientation before applying force.
Hose couplings tightened only by hand often won't hold pressure — or after flowing water, can't be uncoupled without a tool. The spanner ensures proper coupling torque and allows uncoupling under residual pressure. The gas shut-off function adds utility at wildland-urban interface incidents.
Also Known AsSpanner, hose wrench, coupling wrench, lug wrench (fire service context)
🔧
Large Spanner Wrench (5″ Hose / LDH)
Large Spanner / LDH Spanner / 5-Inch Spanner
▶
Same design as the small spanner but sized for large-diameter hose (LDH) couplings — 5-inch Storz or threaded connections. These couplings are heavy and require significantly more torque to tighten properly.
Same technique as the small spanner — insert pin in lug, use as a lever. With 5-inch hose you may need two-handed force and a wide stance to generate enough torque. Always verify couplings are tight before flowing.
Large-diameter hose couplings carry extremely high water volumes and pressures — they cannot be adequately tightened or loosened by hand. An improperly seated LDH coupling can fail catastrophically under pressure. The large spanner is the only practical tool for these connections.
Also Known AsLarge spanner, LDH spanner, 5-inch spanner, big spanner
🔗
Storz Adapters — A through F (Hydrant Bag)
Storz Adapter / LDH Adapter / Hydrant Adapter
▶
A set of labeled connection adapters that allow Storz (sexless, quarter-turn) couplings to interface with threaded NST couplings of various sizes, and vice versa. Storz couplings have no male/female distinction — they are symmetrical and connect with a quarter-turn:

A — Steamer to Storz: Converts hydrant's large 4½-inch NST steamer outlet to Storz coupling.
B — Storz Male (top) / Storz Female: 2½-inch Storz male and female adapters for connecting Storz hose to threaded connections.
C — 2½-inch Hose Adapter: In-line adapter for 2½-inch connection interoperability.
D — 1½-inch Hose Adapter: In-line adapter for 1½-inch connection interoperability.
E — Fire Hose Wrench: Spanner for coupling operations.
F — Double-Ended Spanner: One end fits Storz, the other fits 2½-inch — two tools in one.
  1. Adapter A (Steamer to Storz): Thread the female NST side onto the hydrant's steamer port — hand tight plus a quarter-turn with spanner. Connect your Storz supply hose to the Storz side with a quarter-turn. Open hydrant.
  2. Adapters B–D: Select the correct gender for your connection need. Attach Storz side with a quarter-turn; thread hose coupling with a spanner.
  3. Adapter F (Double-Ended Spanner): Use the appropriate end for your coupling type as a lever to apply torque.
  4. After use: flush all adapters, inspect for damaged threads or Storz ears, store in the labeled hydrant bag slots.
Modern apparatus uses Storz for LDH; older hydrants use threaded outlets. Mutual aid agencies use different standards. These adapters are the universal translation kit — without them, mismatched couplings mean zero water supply regardless of what's available. Know which adapter solves which problem before you need it.
Also Known AsStorz adapter, steamer cap adapter, LDH adapter, hydrant adapter, sexless adapter
🔧
Pipe Wrench
Stillson Wrench / Adjustable Pipe Wrench
▶
An adjustable, serrated-jaw wrench designed to grip and turn pipes, threaded couplings, and round objects. The jaw tightens when torque is applied — the harder you turn, the tighter it grips.
  1. Adjust the jaw opening to just larger than the fitting you need to grip.
  2. Place the jaw so that applying torque will cause it to tighten onto the fitting (the serrations grip better in the tightening direction).
  3. Apply steady pressure — avoid jerking or hammering, which damages fittings.
  4. After use: open the jaw fully before storing — storing under tension damages the adjusting mechanism.
Some hydrant connections, rusty fittings, or improvised supply configurations have round or irregular surfaces that standard spanners can't grip. The pipe wrench gets purchase where other tools can't. It's the problem-solver in the hydrant bag.
Also Known AsStillson wrench, pipe wrench, monkey wrench (loosely)
🖤
Black Electrical Tape
Electrical Tape / Black Tape / Vinyl Tape
▶
Vinyl insulating tape rated for low-voltage electrical applications, stored in the hydrant bag for field utility use.
Use to mark or label hose connections and adapters for quick identification in the field, wrap handles on wrenches for improved grip, or temporarily secure small parts against loss in the bag.
In a bag full of similar-looking adapters in dim light, a piece of tape can distinguish "connected" from "ready," or identify which side of an adapter is inlet vs. outlet. Small tool, prevents confusion at critical moments.
Also Known AsElectrical tape, black tape, vinyl tape, marking tape

🔥 Final Notes from Your Mentor

You made it through the whole truck. That's no small thing.

The truck is a system. Water moves from tank → pump → hose → nozzle. Supply moves from hydrant → adapters → pump. Overhaul moves from tools → fire edge → mop-up. When you understand the system, you can improvise when something doesn't go according to plan — and something never goes according to plan.

Know the "why" better than the "what." Anyone can memorize a list of tools. The firefighter who knows why the suction strainer goes 2 feet under, why you never run the pump dry, and why the wheel chock matters on a slope — that firefighter makes better decisions under pressure.

Do your rig check every single shift. Not because someone is watching, but because the moment you skip it is often the moment something's missing. The compartment check is your pre-flight. Pilots don't skip the pre-flight because the last flight went fine.

Ask questions at the tailboard. Every senior firefighter on your crew has a story about each piece of equipment on this truck — a time they needed it, a time it failed, a time they wished they had it. Those stories are worth more than any study guide. Ask for them.

Study guide prepared for Brushtruck 62 probationary firefighter orientation. Verify all hose lengths, tank capacities, and equipment specifications against your department's current SOPs and apparatus specifications — inventories may change, and your rig is the final authority.

📚 How to Use This Guide

Every piece of equipment on Engine 61 has a job. Your job is to know where it lives, what it does, and how to put it to work before someone tells you to. Use this guide before every compartment check until you can walk the rig blindfolded.

⚡

E61 vs. E62 — Know the Differences

READ THIS FIRST — before you ever ride E61
⚠️
Critical — Don't Mix These Up If you've been training on E62, pay close attention here. Several compartments are in different spots, and the airbag system is different. Grabbing the wrong tool in the wrong spot costs lives.
DIFF-01
Driver's Side Over-Wheel Compartment
AKA: Wheel well compartment
+
📋E61 Has

Pry Axe (Officer's Tool) — E61 stores the pry axe / officer's tool here, over the driver's-side wheel.

📋E62 Has

Air Bags — E62 stores its airbags in this same over-wheel location. E61 does NOT.

📍Where are E61's Air Bags?

E61 stores its air bags in Compartment 3, bottom shelf — near the back on the driver's side. Don't go hunting for them over the wheel on this rig.

DIFF-02
Air Bag Controllers — E61 vs. E62
AKA: Air bag control box, inflation controller
+
🔧What to Know

E61 and E62 use different air bag controller models. The controller stays with its bags — do not swap them between rigs. That said, both systems inflate to 118 PSI maximum safe operating pressure.

⚠️
Never Exceed 118 PSI Overpressure can cause a bag to rupture or blow out from under a load. Always monitor the controller gauge and stop inflation when the load is stabilized, not when the gauge maxes out.
DIFF-03
RIT Pack — E62 Only
AKA: Rapid Intervention Team pack, PASS pack
+
📋Know the Difference

E62 carries a RIT pack on the top shelf of the rear compartment. E61 does not have a RIT pack. If you're riding E61 and get assigned a RIT role, coordinate with command regarding which rig is supplying that equipment.

Hose Line Equipment
CAB-01
Trash Line — 100 ft, 1¾" Preconnected
AKA: Minuteman line, trash pack, bump line
+
📖What it is

A preconnected, 100-foot 1¾" attack line stored in the front cab area. It's the fastest line to pull for small, quick-knockdown fires.

❓Why it's needed

Speed matters. For dumpster fires, small vehicle fires, or any quick knock-down scenario, the trash line gets water flowing without pulling the full crosslay.

🔧How to use
  1. Confirm pump is charged and line is bled.
  2. Grab the preconnected coupling — it's ready to go.
  3. Advance the line toward the fire, keeping slack manageable.
  4. Open nozzle smoothly — avoid the water hammer of a sudden burst.
Watch: 1¾" Hose Advancement
CAB-02
1¾" Crosslay — 200 ft, Fog Nozzle (×2)
AKA: Minute-man load, crosslay, pre-connect
+
📖What it is

Two 200-foot 1¾" attack lines stored in the side/middle hose bed, loaded as crosslays so they can be pulled from either side of the truck. Each comes with a fog nozzle.

❓Why it's needed

The bread-and-butter residential attack line. 1¾" flows about 150–180 GPM — enough to knock down most structure fires with good mobility.

🔧How to use
  1. Grab the nozzle end from whichever side you're working.
  2. Pull the hose straight off the bed — the crosslay feeds off itself.
  3. Advance with your partner while maintaining a working loop.
  4. Fog nozzle: straight stream for penetration, wide fog for knockdown and exposure protection.
✅
Rookie TipDon't pull the entire load at once — take what you need to reach the door, then have your partner feed the line. Dragging excess hose through a structure wastes energy and creates trip hazards.
Watch: Crosslay Deployment
CAB-03
2½" Crosslay — 200 ft, Smooth Bore Nozzle
AKA: Big line, two-and-a-half, deuce-and-a-half
+
📖What it is

A 200-foot 2½" attack line with a smooth bore nozzle. Heavy-caliber attack — flows 250+ GPM at working pressure.

❓Why it's needed

When a 1¾" line isn't going to cut it — commercial structures, large volume fires, or when you need reach and penetration that fog can't provide. Also used for exterior master-stream support.

🔧How to use
  1. This line requires at least 2 firefighters to advance safely.
  2. Smooth bore: no pattern adjustment — aim matters. Point at the base of the fire.
  3. Coordinate closely with the pump operator — this line demands significantly more pressure.
⚠️
Nozzle ReactionA 2½" line at full flow will knock you off your feet if you're not set. Get your stance right — feet staggered, nozzle person braced, backup person directly behind pushing forward. Never open this line solo.
Watch: 2½" Line Advancement
CAB-04
5" Supply Hose — 25 ft (Front) + 1,000 ft (Rear Middle)
AKA: Large diameter hose, LDH, five-inch, supply line
+
📖What it is
